properties.COMMENTS: Following the event, the vegetation at the east end of Lake Monoun (Fig. 2) was locally flattened to the ground up to 100 m from the lake. This was ascribed to the action of water, and the extent of vegetation blow-down indicates that the water wave was locally up to 5 m in height above normal lake level. (reference #13035)

Note: references #13041 & #13037 suggest max runup of ~25 m while a 90 m height from a "fountain of water" not tsunami runup, while references #3402, #13036, #13038 suggest ~75 m max tsunami runup.

Reference #3402:
[...] a 'bubble' of about 3 million m3 of carbon dioxide came from the depths of the lake to the surface. "A wave of water was sent crashing across the lake reaching an average height of about 25 m along the southern shore and overtopping a 75 m high promontory" (Freeth, 1988).

Reference #13041:
Survivors from the valley recalled hearing a rumble that lasted about 20 seconds and seeing a fountain of water and foam that rose about 90m above the lake’s surface. A wave at least 24m tall scoured the rocky lake shore (Brown, 2000 Ref #13037).

Reference #13036:
At the time of our visit the areas where the vegetation had been flattened by a wave of water were still clear. To the south of the lake and in the small cove immediately to the east of the spillway a wave had risen to a height of about 25 m. To the east and north-east of the lake there was little evidence of wave damage. The rock wall to the west of the lake showed evidence of recent rock falls and a significant volume of water swept over the 75-m-high promontory at the southern end of the rock wall [...] However, only about 10 m to the west of the spillway, where the bank is about 2 m above lake level, the vegetation was slightly flattened, suggesting that a small amount of water had slopped over [...] A wave from the north-east could have been reflected and concentrated by the rock wall to the west of the lake in such a way as to overtop the 75-m-high promontory to the south-west. It would also have swept south over the delta plain and into the valleys beyond. A wave originating close to the centre of the volcano which blocks the valley to the north-east is consistent with all the observed damage.

This corresponds with an increase in power for frequencies below 0.4 min− 1, i.e., periods greater than 2.5 min, at that time in Fig. 4a, indicating the arrival of the freely propagating tsunami. It was not possible to see any changes in power per frequency at the estimated arrival time for shock waves two to six. The highest point in the island is understood to be occupied by seven households who were relocated from the old village site in 2020. properties.COMMENTS:
Tsunami activity from Tonga left many boats underwater at Tutukaka Marina. The damage to a Northland marina from the Tongan tsunami is expected to cost millions to repair, but fuller figures won’t be known until next month. Tutukaka marina saw at least 50 damaged or written-off boats, marina piles that needed replacing or reviewing, and an entire berth ‘finger’ that broke loose of the marina when the tsunami struck after the Hunga-Tonga-Hunga-Ha’apai volcano erupted earlier this month [...]One major expense was the fuel pontoon, which was completely washed away and needed to be reinstalled. (reference #13146)

The Tongan tsunami surge that hit Tutukaka causing New Zealand's worst marina tsunami damage bill has resulted in a more than $5.8 million of insurance claims. Insurance Council of New Zealand (ICNZ) chief executive Tim Grafton, said Tutukaka Marina insurance claims from the January tsunami surge totalled $5,876,560 [USD 3.973454 million]. The summer weekend event wrecked large parts of the marina and destroyed many boats - creating New Zealand's worst marina tsunami destruction. More than $3.862m of insurance claims has come after damage to the marina itself. Claims totalling $1.947m were also made for 49 damaged boats. Grafton said there were total of 60 claims from the tsunami surge that hit after the Hunga Tonga- Hunga Ha'apai volcano exploded underwater. These included for boats in the water and trailer craft as well as a vehicle.[...] Claims for damage to the marina itself including to piers and piles make up about 65 per cent of the overall total claim value. (reference #13176)

The small marina at Tutukaka on the north-east coast of New Zealand is a well-known tsunami ‘hotspot’16 and incurred severe damage during this event. The harbor estimates damages from Saturday’s tidal event to be as much as $6.5 million [...] Damages from Saturday’s event include utility infrastructure, damaged pilings and facilities such as restrooms and showers. Waves from the tsunami flooded the restrooms and showers in the harbor with more than 3 feet of water, according to Port Commission Chairman Reed Geisreiter. Additionally, the waves knocked out the power throughout the harbor docks, a place where many people live aboard their moored boats [...] Cost estimates also include embankment repairs on the eastside of the harbor and “unknown but expected” damage to the sea wall on the west side of the harbor. (reference #13160)

Farther north, in Santa Cruz harbour, USA, waves were first observed at 15:00 UTC (07:00 local time). The seventh tsunami crest after this time was the largest, arriving near high tide at 16:50 UTC (08:50 local time). This surge flooded parking lots and damaged vehicles, docks, bathrooms, dredging equipment and other infrastructure around the harbour. This damage was mainly the result of flooding of on-land facilities, which differs from the in-water infrastructure impacts experienced in Ventura harbour. However, during the highest-elevation tsunami crest, floating docks in the rear of Santa Cruz harbour were less than 30 cm from the tops of the piles, implying that a similar event at a slightly higher tide or sea level would have led to widespread destruction in the harbour. (reference #13344)

properties.COMMENTS:
The effects of a tsunami near Tonga Saturday caused at least 22 areas of damage at Ventura Harbor and capsized a boat, harbor officials said. Ventura Harbormaster John Higgins said Sunday that tidal surges a day earlier reached 10 knots and created a 6-foot differential between high and low tide, extremes that contributed to the destruction [...] Around 11 a.m. Saturday, a patrol boat tied to a dock outside the harbor patrol headquarters got swept by the current, swamped by water and capsized [...] Shortly after dark, a 90-foot dock with two boats attached came loose from its pilings in the Ventura Keys, Higgins said. The dock and two vessels – a 70-foot yacht and a 20-foot electric boat called a duffy – broke away from its pilings and struck a second 30-foot dock with another boat. (reference #13161)

The next day, amid a still-tempestuous current, a boat outside the harbor had reported a 10-foot chunk of the runaway concrete dock floating out at sea.(reference #13162)

Ventura Harbor - $1-2 million in damage to 20 docks and a harbor patrol boat which sunk due to strong currents (reference #13181)

In the far field, tsunami impacts were observed and recorded by the authors at Ventura harbour, United States during the day on 15 January 2022. The leading crest of the air-pressure pulse arrived in Ventura at 11:54 UTC (03:54 local time), or 7.65 h after the explosion, and shortly thereafter initial oscillations in the harbour were detected. Larger waves started to arrive near 15:30 UTC (07:30 local time), with the peak intensity of the waves and associated damage observed in the late morning to afternoon on 15 January [...] Most of the damage to fixed infrastructure occurred at low tide (22:51 UTC), or 11 h after the initial waves reached the harbour. Strong and swirling currents19 destroyed three major docks, including a 27 m section of dock attached to four pilings, a commercial dock holding multiple slips and a 9 m residential dock. Additionally, a total of 23 residential floating dock ramps were lifted from supports and carried out by the currents. (reference #13344)

properties.COMMENTS: In Oxnard, Sgt. Dan Smock of Channel Islands Harbor Patrol said Sunday the harbor had no issues. "In Channel Islands (Harbor), we saw about a 4-foot surge coming in and out, but no reported damage," he said. Key design differences tend to spare the Oxnard harbor from damage, he said. An outside detached break wall dampens the effect of swells, two beaches – Kiddie and Hobie – by their location also absorb waves and a dog-leg design from open ocean into the greater harbor dissipates wave energy among other things, Smock noted. (reference #13161)

One Puget Islander was killed and damages estimated as exceeding $70,000 resulted Saturday at 1:20 a.m. when a piece of the hill across the Columbia river from the Island fell off. Haakon Gabrielsen, 59, was killed when the slide-caused wave of water hit his house located outside the dike near the power tower. His house was demolished and his personal effects were scattered over a wide area on the inside or the dike. Mrs. Anton Olsen escaped serious injury when the force of the wave pushed her house from the outside to the inside of the dike. Porches on the Fred Aegerter and Tom lrving homes were hit by the water carried debris. The Tom Irving family heard rocks fall all evening. At 1:20 a.m. the Irvings heard a roar like an earthquake. Mrs. Irvin looked outside and saw water rushing around the house. The wave left, logs etc. in the yard, damaged the skirting or the house, took out the fill leading to the house and put rip-rap rock onto the dike. Power lines of the Wahkiakum County Public Utility District No. 1 were damaged to an estimated $4,000 to $5,000. County Engineer Paul Bourgault estimated damage to the dike road as unofficially at $4,800. On the Oregon side a portion of the Spokane-Portland..Seattle railroad track was washed into the river. Reference #13179:
Official revised records of a U.S. Navy Court of Inquiry concluded that the 29 August 1916 destruction of the armored cruiser USS Memphis anchored off Santo Domingo (Ciudad Trujillo) harbor of the Dominican Republic, Island of Hispaniola, was probably caused by a “tropical disturbance”, a “seismic storm”, or a “tsunami”. However, the present analysis of this naval disaster documents that the loss of the ship was not due to any of these causes, but to rogue waves of a meteotsunami generated from a rapid, significant and progressive drop in atmospheric pressure which begun in the area around August 22 and was associated with a passing hurricane which at its closest point was about 250 nautical miles to the south [...] analysis is based on careful examination of the ship’s log, and on observations of events by the crew and people on the shore [...] The study concludes that it was this significant meteotsunami wave, with augmentation by storm-generated swells that engulfed the USS Memphis at 1640 hour in the afternoon of 29 August 1916 - breaking the chains of its anchors and wrecking it on the rocks of Santo Domingo.

Forty-three people lost their lives that fateful afternoon. Twenty-five crewmembers died when the ship's motor launch capsized in huge breakers at about 14:00, as it was attempting to return to the ship. Another eight members of the crew were lost when three boats sent to sea sank or were wrecked attempting to reach shore after dark. Ten more died either by being washed overboard or from burns and steam inhalation when the ship's boilers exploded. The total casualties, numbered 43 dead and 204 injured.

properties.COMMENTS: Tsunami height was recorded by the tide gauge with height 42 cm in Gelendzhik (50 km south) and 10 cm in Feodosia (60 km across in the Crimean Peninsula). (reference #4213)

Recorded mareograms in stations Gelendzik, Tuapse, Opasnoe, Feodosia, Yalta, Batumi, Mariupol and Kerch. Tsunami amplitude in Gelendzik 20-25 cm. Tsunami intensity I. (reference #4139)

Tsunami height was recorded by the tide gauge with height 42 cm in Gelendzhik (50 km south) and 10 cm in Feodosia (60 km across in the Crimean Peninsula). We should point out that the tsunami record at Gelendzhik is best among all other records in the Black Sea. The record will be shown in the following sections. The intensity of this tsunami can be considered as intensity III–V according to the new tsunami intensity scale of Papadopoulos and Imamura [2001]. (reference #4213)

At Wafer Bay on Cocos Island witnesses filmed the tsunami running upriver and reported strong currents which were not predicted by the model. The contrast between these effects and the small height recorded at the nearby gauge, together with the effects of previous tsunamis, such as the one that occurred in Japan in 2011, confirmed a local effect at Wafer Bay. (reference #13228)

properties.COMMENTS:
The 1-m tsunami in Yevpatoriye is noteworthy; it flooded the embankment for several seconds...(reference #223)

A strong tidal wave as high as 1m near the town of Evpatoria.” (reference #9391)

“In Eupatoria, a short-term strong tidal wave up to 1 m in height appeared, which flooded the embankment” (Smirnov, 1931). “In the city of Eupatoria, the wave damaged the wall of a house” (Polumb, 1933). (reference #12050)

Fast receding of the sea of about 2 m in Sudak and 1-m high tide in Yevpatoriya was observed [Nikonov, 1997]. (reference #4213)

“Town of Sudak: a violent horizontal recession of the sea by 2m and a slow return to the ordinary level in 10 min. A strong tidal wave as high as 1m near the town of Evpatoria.” (reference #9391)

In Sudak, “the sea quickly retreated for a sazhen along the whole coast ..., and then returned to the previous level.” (reference #12050)

Fast receding of the sea of about 2 m in Sudak and 1-m high tide in Yevpatoriya was observed [Nikonov, 1997]. (reference #4213)

Strong sea swell damaging many vessels in the Odessa harbor. (reference #9391)

Odessa: “The earthquake of the 11th day (the old style) was felt on ships standing in the harbor; its effect on the sea is compared with the impact on the ship when it strikes an offshore shoal” (Northern..., 1838). “Many of the ships in the harbor suffered from the great agitation of the sea” (Passek, 1963, pp. 243–244). (reference #12050)

“Sea rose above the ordinary level near the town of Odessa by more than 10 cm; k=II.” (reference #9391)

The authors [Papadopoulos et al. (2011) (reference #9391)] support this last hypothesis and say that the sea disturbance could be attributed equally either to a submarine slump or to a seiche. (reference #11164)

A submarine landslide occurred about 15 km far form the coast and after some minutes in Marseille, at the Pointe Rouge, the sea withdrew for about 20 m, so that the sea level in the harbour lowered for about 50 cm . The phenomenon lasted for about 30 min (BRGM, 2013). (reference #11164)

According to BRGM (2013) , who quotes several coeval sources, on June 25 in the evening, during calm weather, the water in the Marseille harbour considerably retreated, then after 15 min the water came back rapidly and with such a violence that many vessels in the harbour were shaken. After few minutes the sea water rose up to 5-6 feet, inundating the quay. Further references: Lambert and Terrier (2011). (reference #11164)

A slight tsunami was recorded at Acapulco. (reference #1039)

The main shock caused a small tsunami which was recorded at Acapulco. (reference #13231)

properties.COMMENTS: At Ancona, an eyewitness on the beach noted sudden waves coming from the sea that was previously calm (L’Arena 1875). (reference #9531, #11164, #12905)
At Cervia, the sea violently flooded a large stretch of beach, and a remarkable increase in wave motion was observed in the harbours of Cesenatico, Cervia and Pesaro. (reference #9531)
In the canal at the harbor of Cesenatico a remarkable increase in wave motion was observed (Serpieri 1876). (reference #11164)
n increase in wave motion was also observed at Pesaro and an increase in the harbour was observed (Serpieri, 1876). (reference #11164)

At Tavollo tsunami waves observed (reference #4139)

At Tavollo, close to Pesaro, a fisherman who was in his boat about 700 m from the shore said that the sea was calm until suddenly he noted four waves about 20 cm high travelling from the open sea towards the beach. When the waves came to his boat, his fishing tool moved and rose from the sea bottom. Then, the waves reached the beach (Alfani 1916; Boschi et al. 1997; Corriere della Sera 1916; La Gazzetta di Parma 1916) (Fig. 9). (reference #9531)

[...] accompanied by a strong tsunami in the harbour of Ancona (Boschi et al. 1995): Suddenly, high tide impinged on the coast, and the sea boiled. The tsunami waves broke off the moorings of an American ship and slammed it against the dock. The fence of the harbour office was almost completely pulled out, and the docks were heavily damaged. Many fishermen who were on their vessels in the harbour quickly disembarked, frightened by the extraordinary movement of the water (Il Corriere Padano 1930; Il Messaggero 1930) (Fig. 10).(reference #9531)
According to Bonito (1691), in the beach of Ancona the boats touched the sea bottom and then they lifted up being shaken due to the sea water agitation. (reference #11164)

When I [Kispatic] went several hours later (to Bijela), I saw that as I went further, the sea, while it was agitated, came more and more inland. In several places, it went vertically up by 2 stopa, at other places by 3 and in other places by 4 stopa; between two torrents...the sea went up by 5 to 6 stopa, wetting the coast by 8–9 koracaj (ital. passo, about 1.7 m), that is up to the vineyards. Because of that, I believe that, in places where the sea is shallow, at the first shocks the sea must have withdrawn from the coast by 10–12 koracaj, because while coming back, it reached just as much inland. I noticed in this area... that the coast went down by two yards into the sea, in the length of 50 koracaj. All this makes me believe that the power of earthquake was strongest here’. This fine first-hand description of retreat and flooding provides reliable data on a previously unknown tsunami event in the Adriatic. (reference #9531)

At Ortona only one oscillation observed, starting at 11h 30m am with a withdrawal of 15 m. The water came back at 12h. (reference #4139)

At Ortona only one oscillation was observed, with a withdrawal of 15 m. (reference #10285)

At Molfetta a 10m withdrawal was noticed. The period was 5 min. (reference #10285)

At Molfetta at 5.00 am 10 m of withdrawal. The period was 5 min. (reference #4139)

At Termoli the sea withdrew by tens of metres leaving the harbour dried and then violently came back; some swimmers referred that the sea water suddenly became cold and immediately after became also turbolent and strongly agitated (Il Messaggero, 1978) (reference #4139, #10285)

At Bari the sea water suddenly withdrew many times leaving the seafloor dried; some moored ships in the harbour went aground and some fish was found on the beach. At Bari and Vieste the sea suddenly withdrew by about 50–100m leaving boats aground and after a few minutes the sea violently inundated the shore with very high waves, causing damage to the boats and some injured people. The sea water swept away the beach-umbrellas (Il Messaggero, 1978; Il Corriere Adriatico, 1978). (reference #10285)

At Bari the sea water suddenly witdrew many times leaving the seafloor dried; some moored ships in the harbour went aground and some fish was found on the beach (Anonymous). Parenzan (ref #9287) reports that at Bari and Vieste the sea suddenly withdrew for about 50-100 m leaving boats aground and after a few minutes the sea violently inundated the shore with very high waves, causing damage to the boats and some injured people. (reference #4139)

Parenzan (ref #9287) reports that at Bari and Vieste the sea suddenly withdrew for about 50-100 m leaving boats aground and after a few minutes the sea violently inundated the shore with very high waves, causing damage to the boats and some injured people. The sea water swept away the beach-umbrellas. (reference #4139)

At Bari and Vieste the sea suddenly withdrew by about 50–100m leaving boats aground and after a few minutes the sea violently inundated the shore with very high waves, causing damage to the boats and some injured people. The sea water swept away the beach-umbrellas (Il Messaggero, 1978; Il Corriere Adriatico, 1978). (reference #10285)

In many islands and places along the Yugoslavian coasts the sea water suddenly rose; at Vela Luka (Korcula island) the waves were 8m high, inundating the first floors of all the buildings on the shore. Many ships suffered severe damage and the sea water flooded the cost by 650m inland. (reference #10285)

In the early morning of 21 June 1978, Vela Luka on the island of Korcula was flooded by a series of exceptional sea waves. The first wave packet arrived at 5 h 5 min am; the oscillations had a period of 10–20 min and lasted 3 h. At the peak of the event, they had a trough-to-crest height of 6 m. There were no casualties, but the town suffered great damage. The phenomenon occurred, with somewhat less intensity and at roughly the same time, in a number of ports between Split and Dubrovnik. (reference #9531)

Several newspapers reported the effects of the tsunami along the Montenegrin coast (Fig. 27). At the time of the earthquake, sailors at sea felt a shock: ‘From the vessel Ljuta, which was on anchor one mile away from Bar, captain Kaskovic ́ informed that the earthquake was also felt at sea very strongly’ (Slobodna Dalmacija 1979). The effects were much stronger at the coast: ‘In the port of Bar, the Sunday earthquake crashed against the bank a large Italian ocean ship, which then stranded as if it were an egg shell’ (Vjesnik 1979), and ‘... policemen at Ulcinj told us that at the time of the earthquake, the sea receded for 3 m away from the coast ...’ (Vecernji list 1979, of 16/04). (reference #9531)

from newspaper reports, we know that the Montenegro tsunami took at least one casualty in Boka Kotorska: ‘Life on ruins. (Branimir Vucetic) was maintaining his boat on the coast, while Luka Cvijetkovic (58) and schoolboy Dusko Tripkovic (8) were watching him. When the earth shock, the student Vucetic grabbed the boy Tripkovic and they found a shelter by the side of road edge. ...They did not notice when a water wave 3 meter high came behind their backs. In a furious blast, the sea ‘‘swallowed’’ 50 m of road, but also the three of them. The whirl pulled them to the bottom, where the student Vucetic got caught by something hard. Somehow he managed to free himself and dived out where at the surface he found the boy Tripkovic and saved him from the certain death. Sadly, he could not help Luka Cvijetkovic. He saw him in a whirl for a moment, and later his body was found 2 km away’ (Vecernji list 1979, of 21 and 22/04). Let us mention that this newspaper report reveals that the Montenegro tsunami was much stronger than was previously believed on the basis of a tide-gauge record in Boka Kotorska (Soloviev et al. 2000). (reference #9531)

Local tsunami reported in Kotor Bay causing considerable damage. (reference #1053)

The tsunami waves crossed the Adriatic quickly over the South Adriatic Pit, and the tide gauge at Bari recorded oscillations (Fig. 26; Zore-Armanda 1988) of about a 10 cm initial wave height, roughly 30-min period, which continued for at least a day. (reference #9531)

properties.COMMENTS:
A tsunami was observed on the shore from Messina to Syracuse. At first the sea receded from the coasts in Messina, Catania, Augusta, Syracuse and in other places. In Augusta, the sea receded by 25-30 yards and then returned having risen 2.5m above its usual level. (reference #2130)

At Augusta and Siracusa the sea retreated of about 60 m and 100 m, respectively, then returned with a wave reaching heights of about 12 m. Galley ships of the Knights of Malta, anchored in the harbor of Augusta, ran aground on the seabed due to the waves [...] The Augusta area was subjected to the worst combined effect of earthquake and tsunami inundation during the 1693 AD event and references therein, with severe damages and local seismic amplification [...] (reference #13244)

At Augusta the first sea recession drained the harbour completely, causing severe damage to the ships, especially to two large vessels coming from Malta, which violently touched the sea bottom. During the following inundation, the sea submerged the district close to the port as far as the S. Domenico monastery (Acquaviva, 1693; Boccone, 1697a, b, c; Mongitore, 1743; Anonymous, 1693d; Burgos, 1693; Muglielgini, 1695) that was located about 150 m from the sea, and killed many of those people, especially women and children, who, alerted by the big foreshock of two days before, where camping near the pier (Anonymous, 1693e). The sea rose for about 15 m above its usual limit (Mongitore, 1743). (reference #11164, #12905)
At Agnone the sea withdrew and then violently came back exceeding its usual limit (Boccone, 1697a). (reference #11164, #12905)

A tsunami was observed on the shore from Messina to Syracuse. At first the sea receded from the coasts in Messina, Catania, Augusta, Syracuse and in other places [...] in Catania the sea came to the S. Filippo square and flooded farmsteads and buildings in suburbs of the city. (reference #2130).

In the Catania harbor, several historical documents reported a double withdrawal of about 100 m leaving boats stranded on the sea-floor and references therein. When the sea returned, the wave flung the boats beyond the walls, into the town. (reference #13244)

At Catania remarkable a sea level rise (Burgos, 1693) and withdrawal carrying a lot of boats (Campis, 1980; Anonymous, 1693a, b) was observed. For about 15 min. a sequence of waves was noted and three of them almost lapped the city walls. The sea water inundated the town penetrating in San Filippo square; farms located near the town were inundated (Boccone, 1697a). (reference #11164, #12905)
At Lipari Island the sea was very agitated and it flooded the beach (Guidoboni et al., 2018). (reference #11164, #12905)

In Mascali, the sea receded from the coast and subsequently flooded dry land over a distance of more than a mile (reference #2130)

At Mascali the sea flooded the shore for about 1 mile (about 1,5 km) inland (Boccone, 1697a). (reference #11164, #12905)

In the Mascali area, mostly in the proximity of Gurna lagoon (Fig. 12), a double withdrawal of about 800 m was reported by Boccone and Baratta. (reference #13244)
At Mazzarelli (today Marina di Ragusa) the sea withdrew and then it came back violently causing damage to a moored boat (Guidoboni et al., 2018). (reference #11164, #12905)

A tsunami was observed on the shore from Messina to Syracuse. At first the sea receded from the coasts in Messina, Catania, Augusta, Syracuse and in other places. Ground was uncovered in Messina harbour; fish were left at the sea-front after the tsunami (reference #2130)

At Messina, at La Cittadella fortress, 3 sea withdrawals and returns were observed (Anonymous, 1693a): the sea withdrew for 60 paces (about 50 m) and then it violently came back overtaking the dock of the pier. A lot of fish was found on the beach (Boccone, 1697a). (reference #11164, #12905)

A tsunami was observed on the shore from Messina to Syracuse. At first the sea receded from the coasts in Messina, Catania, Augusta, Syracuse and in other places. In Syracuse, the sea receded from the coast three times and each time, it flooded the shore 50 yards farther than the usual surf line. (reference #2130)

At Augusta and Siracusa the sea retreated of about 60 m and 100 m, respectively (reference #13244)

At Siracusa three fluxes and refluxes were observed: according to Boccone (1697a), the sea in the harbor withdrew and the sea bottom remained dried for about 50 paces (more than 70 m); then the sea level rose for more than 8 feet (about 2.5m) respect to its usual level. For about 15 days after the shock fishermen that usually cast the net at a depth of 15 "paces of rope" noted that they could reach the sea bottom with only 5 paces of rope. (reference #11164, 12905)

At Taormina (Giardini Naxos) the sea withdrew for about half a mile dragging some small boats (Boccone, 1697a). (reference #11164, #12905)

in Taormina the sea receded for a mile (reference #2130)
A sea-wave was observed in Galaxidi. (reference #2130)
In the beaches of Malfa and Capo in Salina Island an anomalous sea movement was observed, with sea water firstly receding (Cavasino, 1935). (reference #3078, #11164)

On the beaches of Malfa and Capo Faro, in Salina island, a light tsunami was observed with an initial withdrawal of the sea (Cavasino, 1935). Newspapers reported detailed information on the earthquake, but gave no mention of anomalous sea behaviour. (reference #3078, #11164)

Abbruzzese (1936) reports that at Piscita in the Eolo's grotto a fisherman who was trying to take shelter from the rain of burning lava, run towards the sea. An anomalous wave invested him and the water, boiling hot due to the heat of the lava that had come in contact with the sea, caused him some mortal scolds. (reference #11164)

At Piscita, in the Eolo’s grotto, a fisherman, who was trying to take shelter from the rain of burning lava, ran towards the sea and a wave, boiling hot due to the heat of the lava that had come in contact with the sea water, attacked him causing mortal scolds (Abruzzese, 1936). (reference #3078)

Note: death at Piscita due to the heat of the lava that had come in contact with the sea water, not attribute to tsunami in NCEI database

A hot avalanche at the Forgia Vecchia reached the beach were big waves were noted (Ponte, 1948). (reference #11164)

A hot avalanche at the Forgia Vecchia, on the opposite side of the island, reached the coast where big waves were noted. Eyewitnesses reported that the beach was full of fish (Ponte, 1948). (reference #3078)
The wave was about 1 meter high on land at Eratini and flooded the lower parts of the village (reference #13256)

Reference #4727:
It was estimated that between the lighthouses Punta Corona and Punta Ahui this mass of water had a height of about 15 meters. This observation was made by several people, among them the master of a sailing ship that had been drawn away during the withdrawal of the sea, who at one moment compared the height of the mass of water with that of the mast of his ship. In its advance toward the south, the wave struck with great force along the northeast coast of Peninsula Lacui.
Chilean accounts report unusual sea movements, including a slight withdrawal and anomalous tides, in Concepcion; a bay that usually amplifies tsunamis. (reference #13286)

One month later the ship anchored at Lemu Island and the captain observed the results of the earthquake. “On the 11th of December, 1837, he came to resume his anchorage near the island of Lemus. The shock of the 7th of December had raised the bottom more than 8 feet [2.5 m]”. The evidence of such changes was conspicuous: “Some rocks, which formerly had been always covered by the sea, now remained constantly exposed”. Whether a result of the uplift or the tsunami, Coste saw signs that proved to himself the changes to the island. “An enormous quantity of shells, and fish in a state of decomposition, thrown on the shore either by a sudden elevation or by the oscillations of the sea, showed that the event had been of recent occurrence”. The 1837 tsunami may also have left its imprint on Lemu: “A great quantity of trees, torn up by the roots and carried to sea in those shocks, were to be seen along the shore”. (reference #13286)

properties.COMMENTS: In a surprising quirk of geology, Monday’s magnitude 7.6 earthquake in Mexico triggered four-foot-tall waves in Devils Hole, located in Death Valley National Park. The earthquake shook the Mexican states of Colima and Michoacán at 11:05 am Pacific Daylight Time. Twenty-two minutes later, water started sloshing 1,500 miles away in Devils Hole. The waves reached 4 feet high around 11:35 am. Devils Hole is a partially water-filled limestone cave in a Nye County, Nevada unit of Death Valley National Park. (reference #13332)

Peru Environment Minister Ruben Ramirez said on Monday the government will temporarily suspend Repsol's offshore oil unloading operations following a spill of over 10,000 barrels that has caused widespread environmental damage. The spill took place on the Pacific Ocean just off the coast of Lima on Jan. 15, which the company has blamed on unusual waves triggered by a volcanic eruption thousands of miles away in Tonga. Peru's government has said the spill involved 11,900 barrels of oil, while the company said the number was smaller, involving 10,396 barrels. (reference #13144)

In the nearby La Pampilla oil terminal the oil tanker vessel Mare Doricum reported the breaking of mooring ropes, which led to an oil release of approximately 6,000 barrels. By international standards, this is classified as a large oil spill (reference #13344)

properties.COMMENTS:
For the 1839 earthquake, we find the first description of an anomalous behavior of the sea in “Le chapelier pirate”(Peray, 1843, p.327; ref#13360) saying “Plus terrible encore, la mer bouleversée se présenta dans une position déversante sur toute la ville et eut le temps de gagner dix à quinze mètres sur elle, mais, fort heureusement, le mouvement se fit en sens inverse plus promptement que par la parole. . . ”, which can be translated as “Even more terrible, the shook up sea rose to cover all the city in a pouring position and had time to gain ten to fifteen meters on it, but, very fortunately, the sea withdraw more quickly than time allowed. . . ”. (reference #12203) (Note: reference #13359 clarifies that the 10-15 meters are inundation, not runup/height)

Regarding the seismic event of 11 January 1839, [reference #12203] found a description in the book Le chapelier pirate of an anomalous behavior of the sea with flooding, within the bay of Fort-de-France, western Martinique. (reference #13356)
The impact, at 9:23 am (Italian time) triggered a small tsunami wave recorded on all four sensors of the two Elastic Beacons placed on the sides of the Sciara del Fuoco.

The impact, at 9:23 am (Italian time) triggered a small tsunami wave recorded on all four sensors of the two Elastic Beacons placed on the sides of the Sciara del Fuoco. This is the fourth (small) tsunami recorded by the Medes since July 2019. The tsunami wave has a first positive impulse of about 2 cm, consistent with an underwater origin of the source, followed by a negative amplitude of about 5 cm produced by the call of water towards the impact zone. Amplitude and time of arrival at the two Mede coincide and indicate a source area equidistant to the sensors, consistent with the images of the surveillance cameras in the central portion of the Sciara. The preliminary localization indicates a distance of about 1100 m from the Mede and a propagation speed of about 32 m / s. (reference #13357)

A primary source of the tsunami is Mr Gervacio Evangelista who was 28 years old in 1948. Mr Evangelista was then residing in Bgy Tando in the town of Nueva Valencia in Guimaras Island. During the earthquake, he was on board a boat called “Batel Cornelio” together with five other passengers. The boat was in the shores of Miagao. He recounted that all boat passengers felt the shaking, then they heard a whistling sound. Then, they saw a 2-m high wave. The wave carried their boat towards the shore. The passengers jumped from the boat and upon landing. experienced waist-level flood. (reference #9750) Note: 2 m appears to be offshore

A primary source of the tsunami is Mr Gervacio Evangelista who was 28 years old in 1948. Mr Evangelista lives in Bgy Tando in the town of Nueva Valencia in Guimaras Island. During the earthquake, he was on board a boat called “Batel Cornelio” together with five other passengers. The boat was in the shore of Miagao. The passengers felt shaking, then heard a whistling sound. Then, they saw a 2-m high wave. The wave carried their boat towards the shore. The passengers jumped from the boat and upon landing. experienced waist-level flood. Upon his return home, his wife told him about a wave observed in the island. According to his wife, a “batel” named Flor Batel owned by Mr Juan Ilijan was also carried by the wave (Bautista et al, 2010). (reference #10958)

Note: this tsunami observation was the result of a landslide produced by the magnitude 9.5 earthquake

The tsunami recorded in the Lake Nahuel Huapi, Patagonia Argentina, on May 22, 1960 is the first example of a tsunami in a continental lake in Argentina. [...] The impact of the seismic waves produced huge mass-failure below 70-80 m water depth. The failure was probably induced by the presence of a non-cohesive surface (tephra layer?) that acted as a sliding surface, and the mobilized material evolved into a mega turbidite in the deep basin. A large volume of water was displaced by the mobilization of these sediments producing a tsunami that hit the coasts of Bariloche and destroyed the harbor of the city. (reference #12893)

Lake Nahuel Huapi would recede a few meters and then return with waves five meters high [...] The port was built of wood and was destroyed by the force of the water, which entered more than 100 meters into the city itself, causing damage and widespread panic. As it retreated, the water took with it at least three lives. (Note: unofficial translation) (reference #13368) (Note: deaths are not included in the totals for the earthquake and tsunami events in the NCEI/WDS database)

properties.COMMENTS: [...] the main tsunami of January 15th occurred during the high tide period on Tongatapu and shortly after high tide at Neiafu. At Neiafu tsunami amplitudes were generally smaller than the tide range, while at Nuku’alofa the tsunami amplitudes are more than twice the tide range. properties.COMMENTS:
Inspection of the data from the day before the main eruption shows a period of sea level agitation commencing at approximately 1800 hours on 13 January (UTC) and lasting for approximately 24 hours. The main tsunami event commenced at approximately 0425 hrs (UTC) on January 15 with the highest tsunami water level reaching just under 3.0 m relative to the tide gauge datum. The data from nkfa and nkfa2 closely mirror each other with the tsunami signal on nkfa2 slightly preceding that of nkfa due to its more westerly location [...] the first ~3.5 hours of the de-tided tsunami record at Nuku’alofa (nkfa2). In this plot the vertical red line is the time of the large magnitude explosion of the eruption sequence (USGS, 2022), which occurred at 0415 UTC. Tsunami activity is present on the gauge at ~0425 UTC, just 10 minutes after the explosion – which is too early for water waves generated by it. (reference #13394)

Ref #13394 notes two tide gauges were in operation on the Nuku’alofa waterfront during the tsunami, the ‘nkfa’ sensor at Queen Salote Wharf and ‘nkfa2’ located 1.8 km to the west at the Vuna Wharf. This location is ‘nkfa2’ sensor at Vuna Wharf.

Reference #13397:
Atata and Fafa are small islands located off the northern coast of Tongatapu. Due to their relatively exposed location, they were strongly affected by the tsunami waves. The low-lying peninsula protruding southward from Atata was completely overtopped with tsunami heights of ~6 m (~4 m flow depth). Runup heights on the higher topography of the island were 6-8 m.

The tsunami swept Mr. Folau out to sea at approximately 6 pm on Saturday and he was forced to swim and float on debris, before eventually making his way to the main island of Tongatapu at Sopu at 10 pm on Sunday night. [...] In his account, Mr. Folau describes an initial surge that alerted people on the island to the tsunami, prompting their evacuation. This was followed by a large surge approaching from the northwest that split around the island, wrapping around and meeting on the low peninsula protruding to the south. This surge is described as being 7 m high and highly destructive destroying houses and washing across the island. Mr. Folau and others climbed a tree to escape this surge. After this, there was a period of calm with no waves when they came down from the tree and started to walk to higher ground, helping others to safety as well. After some time, as they were moving, they were alerted by others that another large wave was coming. This surge, also estimated at 6-7 m, washed Mr. Folau into the sea. He grabbed on to debris and floated near the island, hearing people calling for him, but he did not reply, for fear of putting them into danger. After this, he recalls another large surge taking him further from land. He floated through the night before landing on Toketoke around dawn. That morning, from land, He saw police boats going by, but they did not see him despite his signalling. Taking matters into his own hands, he used a piece of plywood as a float and essentially paddled along the shallow reef edge to Polo’a arriving there at dusk on Sunday to find the area abandoned. He carried on, making it to Sopu, west of Nuku’alofa by 10 pm Sunday night where he finally found help and made contact with his family.

properties.COMMENTS:
At Kanokupolu, a weather station co-located on a cellular phone tower situated at approx. +13 m elevation was toppled by the tsunami, ripped from its foundations and transported more than 200 m from its original location. The weather station collected data at 10 min intervals and this data was uploaded every hour on the hour via satellite telemetry. The station made its final transmission at 05:00 UTC (18:00 local) and was therefore destroyed some time after (Fig. S1). Passed from east to west across peninsula (reference #13394)

At Kanokupolu the tsunami overtopped the peninsula flowing across into the lagoon. A weather station positioned on a cell phone tower with base at a ground elevation of approximately 13 m above sea level was destroyed by the tsunami. The station observed the onset of the eruption and reported data until 05:00 UTC (18:00 local time). Three days after the tsunami, a site visit revealed that the tower had been toppled and transported approximately 20 m from its original location, suggesting tsunami flow elevations significantly greater than 13 m above mean sea level. One woman, Angela Glover (51) a British national, was killed in Kanokupolu (Matai Tonga, 2022, Reuters, 2022)

properties.COMMENTS:
Ha’atafu was the scene of remarkable tales of survival (Fig 8a). Moana Paea, proprietor of the Ha’atafu Beach Resort described hearing a commotion from the beach area as the first surges rose above the high tide level, reaching the beachside boundary of the resort. At the same time, Australian High Commissioner Rachael Moore, who was at the resort with her family, observed and photographed these early surges indicating a time of ~0415 UTC (17:15 local) for the first significant waves. Videos shared on social media also show local residents who had been spending the day on the beach, returning to their cars after being chased off the beach by the first surges. Ms. Paea and her staff began alerting other guests to leave the resort, all of whom went to the carpark and began to leave by vehicle. A second video obtained from social media shows the vehicles evacuating as a tsunami surge rushes up the road adjacent to the resort, toppling a fence as it progresses inland and narrowly missing a car full of people that had been parked on the waterfront. As this was going on Ms. Paea, her family and staff, noting the vehicular congestion, fled on foot in search of a large ‘tsunami rock’ they had previously identified as high ground for potential tsunami evacuation. While looking for this rock in the heavily vegetated bush area behind the resort, they felt and heard one of the large explosions and shock waves released during the eruption, noting that ‘it felt like a bomb’ and nearly ‘knocked [us to the] ground’. Unable to locate the ‘tsunami rock’ the group continued by foot to the lagoon side of the peninsula seeking refuge with others on the roof of a house. Their inability to locate the tsunami rock was fortuitous in that the tsunami surges completely overtopped the rock leaving it covered with debris (Fig 8b). (reference #13394, #13397)

At Ha’atafu near the northern tip of the peninsula, locally high topography did not allow for complete overtopping with runup stopping at 13-15 m. Just south of these transects, several beach resorts were located on land at elevations of ~5-7 m. This area was completely overrun by the tsunami which destroyed every structure, reducing reinforced concrete buildings to bare foundations (Figure 3.3). The force of the tsunami also stripped away nearly all the coastal vegetation as shown in Figure 3.4. (reference #13397)

Reference #13394:
Finally, the village on the northern coast of Mango Island was totally destroyed by tsunami runup exceeding 7 m and maximum measured tsunami trace heights of nearly 10 m

Reference #13397:
Two of the three casualties caused by the tsunami occurred in this area, one on Nomuka (Maumi Lauaki) and one on Mango (Telai Tutu‘ila, age 65).
Mango Island was heavily damaged by the tsunami with measured tsunami heights of just under 10 m from two transects taken in the village at the northern end of the island. With the tsunami approach from the west, the village on the north coast was not protected as the wave wrapped around the island. It is also possible that the high tide allowed for stronger refraction and some amplification over the offshore reef platform on the north-western side of the island. News accounts report that all of the residents from Mango were evacuated to Tongatapu after spending the night outdoors.

properties.COMMENTS:
When the sounds of waves and destruction were silent for at least an hour on both Mango and Tungua, the respective town officers organised scouting parties of men to descend and check for damage (and in the Mango case search for a missing person). In both cases ongoing smaller tsunami surges were reported. On Tungua this party arrived near the coast after ~0900 UTC to witness the arrival of a later tsunami wave that inundated low-lying areas approximately one quarter of the maximum runup. (reference #13394)

The village on Tungua is located on the eastern side of the island away from the direction of approach of the tsunami. Furthermore, the island is surrounded by a relatively wide and shallow reef shelf which would have acted to reduce tsunami impacts. Despite these factors, the tsunami inundated over 175 m inland and caused significant damage. Two profiles were measured at Tungua with flow depths of 1-3 m observed along the transect indicating a maximum total tsunami height of ~4 m. Damage on Tungua include a collapsed wood-frame building, concrete structures destroyed, a moved and damaged concrete water tank, damage to a solar panel array and boats damaged and pushed ashore. (reference #13397)

properties.COMMENTS:
The article in Avangnamiok reports the witness account of the surviving fishermen who were working on a barge with fishing nets on the south coast of Nuussuaq, 10 km south-east of the landslide, near Ataa. On the day of the landslide, they were at sea fishing for “whitefish” (beluga whale) for the workers in the coal mine in Qullissat and had caught four. After fishing, they were cleaning their nets on the beach at southern Nuussuaq. The exact location of this is unknown, but as the survivors hiked to a travel hut, which is presumably at Ataa, we assume that the beach was close to this location, around 10 km south of the area of the landslide. At around 14:00 local time, they first saw what they thought was fog slowly dispersing at the site of the landslide and continued cleaning their nets. Then they saw a motorboat being pushed towards them by an iceberg carried by a large wave. The force of the wave lifted their pramto a vertical position in the water, and three of them were thrown up on land above the usual hightide mark. The fourth fisherman was killed in this event and his body was not found until the next day. The three survivors suffered injuries from ice blocks hitting them with the first wave but reached higher ground before a second wave hit the coast. After this they walked in their soaked and frozen clothes (air temperature was reportedly below freezing) to the travel hut at Ataa, where they lit a fire and signalled for help with flares and were later rescued by a search party from Qullissat. In addition to the information on the events near Ataa, the article in Avangnamiok reports the description from an eyewitness on how a group of people visited the site of the landslide the day after the event and how the waves had flooded a small nearby promontory, ripping up the grass and leaving icebergs above the high-water mark.

A previously unnamed landslide on the south coast of Nuussuaq in 1952 generated a tsunami that caused one fatality, and was observed in the mining town of Qullissat on northern Qeqertarsuaq (cites reference #1399). (reference #12607)

According to the eyewitnesses, the sea was boiling in several parts of Argostoli Bay, whirlpools were also observed, while repeated cycles of coastal inundation and sea withdrawal affected several parts of the bay (TAXYDROMOS, 14.08.1953). The waves inundated the coastal area and reached the Argostoli square (ELEFTHERIA, 13.08.1953). Many boats near the waterfront immediately raised their anchors so as not to be damaged by the waves that were triggered by the earthquake (TA NEA, 13.08.1953). This disturbance of the sea was also mentioned by Petratos [46]. Based on information by prisoners in Argostoli prison, a tsunami has flooded the coast of Argostoli Bay [...] (reference #13476)

Press reports based on eyewitness accounts were examined by other authors. The examination showed that during the earthquake, the sea looked like boiling in several parts of Argostoli Bay, while whirlpools were also observed. Several inundation-withdrawal cycles were observed in the bay, and the waves inundated up to the city square, i.e., ~100 m from the seashore. Seaquakes were felt onboard ships in the bays of Argostoli and Vathy, as well as offshore Patras. (reference #13999)

Reference #13476:
A tsunami was triggered by the 11 August 1953 earthquake and affected several coastal areas in Cephalonia, Ithaki and Zakynthos Islands. The most characteristic case was reported in the coastal area of Vathi in Ithaki (ELEFTHERIA, 12.08.1953; EMPROS, 12.08.1953; TO VIMA, 12.08.1953; NEOLOGOS PATRON, 12.08.1953; PELOPONNISOS, 12.08.1953; Figure 8). The waves were one-meter high and inundated a 1-km-long coastal area, to a maximum distance of 200 m from the shore (ELEFTHERIA, 12.08.1953; EMPROS, 12.08.1953). The Customs Office of Vathi was flooded by the inundation (NEOLOGOS PATRON, 12.08.1953). The sea withdrew and then returned to inundate the same area. Similar phenomena were also observed during the aftershock sequence and mainly after its largest seismic events (ELEFTHERIA, 12.08.1953; EMPROS, 12.08.1953)

Reference #13999:
According to a press report, “the beach of Vathy town, Ithaki Island, was flooded by the sea before and after each earthquake at a length of ~200 m and at inland distance of 50 m, thus intensifying the panic”. This description, which indicates that the earthquakes triggered local tsunamis in Vathy Bay, is consistent with an account published by [43] in relation to the earthquake of 9 August. Another set of press reports [44] is also consistent with the previous accounts. Namely, it was reported that in Vathy, the tsunami wave height reached 1 m and inundated the coastal area at the length of 1 km. The wave penetrated inland at a maximum distance of 200 m from the shore. The Customs Office of Vathy was flooded. After the first inundation, the sea withdrew and then returned to inundate the same area. Similar phenomena were also observed in association with other earthquakes of the sequence.

Reference #13476:
The earthquake triggered tsunami, which affectedmainly Vathi in Ithaki Island (Figure 11; EMPROS, 13.08.1953; TAXYDROMOS, 13.08.1953; TANEA, 13.08.1953; NEOLOGOS PATRON, 14.08.1953). The waves inundated the coast and moved further inland, up to the squares of Vathi (NEOLOGOS PATRON, 14.08.1953). Water marks of small seaweed pieces were left on streets of the town, indicating the extended inundation of the coastal area (TA NEA, 13.08.1953). Some people, found along its course were swept away, but no casualties were reported (NEOLOGOS PATRON, 14.08.1953).

Reference #13999:
According to press reports, because of this earthquake, a coastal part of Ithaki Isl. slipped into the sea, and the resulting sea wave inundated the port of Vathy. Other press reports verified the triggering of a tsunami that affected Vathy without referring to the tsunami source type, landslide, or other. The waves inundated the coast and moved further inland, up to the square of the town, where some people were swept away; no casualties were reported. Small seaweed pieces were left as watermarks on the streets of the town.

properties.COMMENTS:
Reference #13478 [unofficial translation of eyewitness account]:
Playa Potrero, Vírgilio Guido, fisherman: Look at Don Guillermo, the tide rises and falls here every ten minutes. You know better than me that this lasts 12 hours, but now that doesn't happen here, since last night. It all started around midnight, the tide came in when it shouldn't, you know it was low tide. We were at the marina dock and suddenly the sea, without warning, rose so much that it was only a meter away from throwing itself into the street, which is very high. In other words, it advanced about 200 meters further inland than normal. In an estuary that is nearby, the water rises and then falls with a great roar, as when a river comes down with a head of water... and that every ten minutes. It's very weird. Please tell us what is happening and what we should do.

Reference #13478 [unofficial translation of eyewitness account]:
Marina Flamingo, Jose Benavente, Coast Guard Marina Flamingo Station: At around midnight, a large wave entered the rad (sic) of the marina, taking with it the dock and the yachts that were moored here. It was a lot of water that turned and took everything... when it went down, it left that very deep area that the bottom could be seen from here. We went down on foot, where there used to be a great depth, we walked knee-deep in water and picked up a boat and brought it back by hand until we tied it up again.

Reference #13478 [unofficial translation of eyewitness account]:
In an interview conducted in March 2021, through our Facebook page, a tourist from Hampton, NH United States of America, who was visiting Tamarindo on March 12, shared photos with us and tells the following: We we were in Tamarindo and the tide was higher than normal and this happened for several days. The Diria (hotel) put sandbags on the wall they have along the coast. The strangest thing was that the tide went up and down like every 20 minutes. After that we found shells on the beach that we had never found before and never found again after that day (...) It definitely happened from the mouth of the river and covered the entire beach.

Reference #13478 [unofficial translation of eyewitness account]:
Marbella, Santa Cruz, Arturo Quiros: From this cliff, I see that the tide rises and falls every 8 minutes. In the distance, the sea is dark in color, like brown, and different algae have emerged that are not the ones on the rocks, they look like they come from the bottom of the sea and are found on some beaches. Here I see some fishermen on the rocks and when the sea rises they run and climb higher; and when the sea goes down they throw the hooks and catch fish, because they walk like crazy. The tide every ten or eight minutes reaches the bushes that are on the shore of the beach, where the tide only reaches the highest ones. The great tide last night came up to the palm trees with pipes. That had never been seen [...]

Reference #13478 [unofficial translation of eyewitness account]:
This morning when we went fishing around 5 in the morning, the sea dried up suddenly, then it filled up very quickly and dried up again. It was like that all morning until around eight when we were able to go out to the boats that were left stranded on the rocks [...]

Reference #13478 [unofficial translation of eyewitness account]:
"Severe variations in sea level began at 6 pm and ended at 10 pm. It was something we have never seen. In the estuaries, the water rose to levels never seen before and with it dropped very quickly, at 10-minute intervals."

Reference #13478 [unofficial translation of eyewitness account]:
"The tide varied abruptly between 9 and 10 at night. It rose and fell uncontrollably, there were a lot of waves."

Reference #13478 [unofficial translation of eyewitness account]:
"Before the earthquake last night, first a very strong north (wind) blew. After the earthquake, the sea got out of control. It was indisposed. It rose and dried, rose and dried, like every 10 minutes ... and still today it did the same ..."

Reference #13478 [unofficial translation of eyewitness account]:
Here we are on the Mata de Limon bridge. We have seen the sea all afternoon. It behaves very strange. Sometimes the current goes inside and 15 minutes later it goes the other way. The sea has never done this. And the curious thing is that there is no swell that can explain this. The sea is calm... By the way, my grandson was fishing last night in the estuary here, on the train bridge. And he told me that the bait they had in the water sometimes went up and sometimes went down with the current, typically this happens every 6 hours, last night it did it every 20 minutes. It's very strange ...
reported very strong waves

Reference #13478 [unofficial translation of eyewitness account]:
Parque Marino Ballena, Juan Luis Sanchez Villarevia, park administrator: At 7am on Friday March 11 (sic) I proceed to close the park to the public, and I instruct those in charge of customer service and all the staff to communicate the action, this is done as we do not have the capacity to evacuate tourists in case of alert. This measure was well received by visitors and residents of the community, users of the park who proceeded to close their trips for that day. On March 12, we proceed to check the beaches in order to detect any anomaly, at about 2 pm it is possible to verify that the "tombolo" [sand spit] was closed at its entrance. In other words, the well-known Moises Pass, which allows entry to the point of Uvita during low tide and was not discovered until mid-tide, preventing visitors from passing through. It is presumed that it may be because the tides for that day, the high is 5.9 feet and the low is 1.4 feet, but without verifying the situation in the field, which will be done the next day.

On Sunday, March 13, we visited the site precisely when the tide was low (14h27'), finding the same situation: the entrance to the tombolo (Moises Pass) is covered by the tide, a situation that until March 10, 2011 it had never happened. Two colleagues proceed to verify the local depth of the new channel in that tidal phase. They manage to determine that the local depth reaches up to 1.20 meters in some sectors and other depths are somewhat less along the channel. The distance that is currently covered by water at low tide is on the order of 300 to 400 meters. Which is now the width of the channel, measured from the mean level of the water on the beach, to the place where the sand bar emerges, for that tidal phase.
reported very strong swell (waves)

At least in Puerto Jiménez at the Public Dock very large eddies were formed, tearing boats from their buoys. This current was heading towards Rincon. These are the data reported by officers of the Puerto Jiménez Public Force and in other posts by MINAET personnel.

Reference #13478 [unofficial translation of eyewitness account]:
In Cabo Matapalo Mr. Kirk Ulbrich reported to me very strong waves and withdrawal from the sea, approximately 30 feet; and then break towards the beach and part of the ZMT. This occurred after 9:30pm on Friday.

Mrs. Jusy Wauters Bustos was at the Occidental Tamarindo Hotel (Langosta beach) at the time of the earthquake and reported that "the sea moved away and stayed like that for half an hour or maybe more since I left, but the next day returned to normality (...) and where the San Francisco estuary or river is, a sandbank was made". This corresponds to a tsunami observation, since it indicates that the next day the sea returned to normal. (reference #13478)

A large rock slide of approximately 200,000 m3 fell into the upper reaches of Gold Arm in Charles Sound (Hancox et al., 2003), generating a local tsunami within the Sound. The landslide occurred on a 40 degree slope, not atypically steep for the Fiordland region, and fell about 350 m into water that reaches a maximum of about 18 m depth. The tsunami propagated 800 m across the sound. On the far side of the sound, vegetation was damaged to a height of 4-5 m above the high-tide level over an area of approximately 0.45 km2. A small island within the sound was partially stripped of vegetation. The tsunami also damaged a helipadwharf about 250 m from the landslide along the same shoreline. (#3830)

properties.COMMENTS:
Reference #9572:
The tsunami impacted the sparsely populated Steep Point coastline close to low tide. It caused widespread erosion in the littoral zone, extensive vegetation damage and destroyed several campsites. Eyewitnesses reported three waves in the tsunami wave train, the second being the largest.
At Steep Point, eyewitness accounts were collected from the ranger in residence and several families who were camping in the area in accordance with UNESCO guidelines (1998). Eyewitnesses consistently reported three waves in the tsunami wave train at approximately 19:30, 19:40 and 20:00 local time (UTC+8 h). In all accounts, the second wave was the biggest. The Steep Point tsunami was described as a ‘‘wall of dark water’’ with a sound ‘‘like the roar of a freight train.’’ Maximum water heights were variously reported between ‘‘knee-high’’ and ‘‘chest-high’’. Although the eyewitnesses were aware that a tsunami had occurred in Indonesia, they received no warning that the West Australian coast might be impacted. When the first tsunami wave arrived, the eyewitnesses self-evacuated to nearby hills.

properties.COMMENTS: Further north at Cleaverville, on the Pilbara coast, a one-metre-high tsunami inundated around 150 m inland at low tide. It was reported to sound ‘‘like an ore train.’’ However, damage was minimal and only a few centimetres of water inundated the nearby caravan park. An extract from the Pilbara News on the 26 July 2006 reports: ‘‘As far as the eye could see there was a wall of white foam about 800 mm to a metre high... the full length of the bay for about 4 or 5 km was one single wave coming in.’ (reference #9572)

properties.COMMENTS:
Reference #9572:
The highest run-up recorded from the 2006 tsunami in Australia occurred at the western end of the sand spit within Shelter Bay on steeply sloping limestone cliffs less than 10 m above high tide.
On the gently sloping low, undulating dunes at Shelter Bay, run-up was in the order of 3 m.
However, a road on the western side of the inundated area acted as a channel for the tsunami and inundation in this region increased to over 200 m from mean high tide.
Based on eyewitness accounts and biological markers, tsunami flow depths were in the order of 1.5–2 m.
Had the tsunami arrived at high tide, considerably larger flow depths, inundation and damage could be expected.
In Shelter Bay, the tsunami had a flow depth of between 1 and 2 m, inundation of up to 200 m inland and run-up of up to 7.9 m AHD.

In 1812 the great earthquake occurred on the California coast and at that time every soul left the island of S. Rosa. The waters receded from the island several hundred yards. This so alarmed the Indians that, fearful that the island was about to be engulfed, they departed and were settled in bands of three or four hundred at the several missions. The above is the story told by the Indian. It is not difficult to read the power of the priests in this abandonment. Doubtless predictions of heavy punishment in case the islanders still proved contumacious, had often been made by the priests, and this earthquake was interpreted by the superstitious Indians as the first of a series of fatal catastrophes. (reference #13541)

One of the last outposts for the Chumash Indians was Santa Rosa Island which the Chumash called Mascui. At the time of the 1812 earthquakes, the Franciscan priests were trying to convince the remaining Chumash Indians to relocate to the missions on the mainland. When the 1812 tsunami at Santa Rosa caused the waters to recede several hundred yards from the island, the Indians became fearful that the island was about to be engulfed, so they abandoned totally their villages. They rowed out to in their oceangoing canoes to the mainland and settled in bands of three or four hundred at the several missions in the area. The Chumash Indians who moved to the missions did not fare well, many of them succumbing to European diseases. (H. W. Henshaw, quoted in Anthropological Records, California Linguistic Records, v. 15, no. 2). (reference #13540)

Note: it is not certain this account relates to the 1812 December 21 event.

properties.LOCATION_NAME: COAST OF THE SECOND KURIL STRAIGHT
properties.COMMENTS: Maximum tsunami run-up heights on the coast of the Second Kuril Strait were estimated visually as 2–2.5 m above the mean sea level. Tsunami waves penetrated river valleys up to 40 m distance from the river mouth.

According to information collected by resident A. Korablev, local inhabitants of the island visiting the former settlement Sentyabrsky on March 11 and 12, 2011 did not see ‘‘any tsunami run-up traces higher than fresh storm traces (1.5–2 m)’’. (reference #10007)

According to resident M. Denisova, tsunami runup near Otradnoye village on the coast of Golovnina Bay did not exceed about half a meter, below which on the morning of 12 March she noticed black beach sand. (reference #10007)
The sea water came close to the house used by ichthyologists located near the Ilyushina River mouth, a run-up of about 2 m above mean sea level. (reference #10007)

In Yuzhno-Kurilsk Harbor Mr. P. Komov, Vice-director of the ‘‘Doker’’ company, reported that the maximum tsunami height of 0.3–0.5 m above the pier occurred between 13:30–14:00 UTC on March 11. This corresponds to a maximum run-up of about 2.2 m above mean sea level. (reference #10007)

Near Goryachy Plyazh settlement, a tsunami run-up height of 1.9 m above mean sea level was estimated by traces of the beach sand deposited by the tsunami on snow in the southern part of Yuzhno-Kurilsk Bay. (reference #10007)

Nazarov, who lives in Golovnino village (southern part of Kunashir Island, Fig. 1), reported that during the tsunami sea water came within about 2 m of his house. Maximum sea water elevation at this time exceeded the maximum tide (?0.67 m) by about 0.7 m resulting in maximum run-up of 1.4 m above mean sea level. (reference #10007)
Maximum tsunami run-up height in Khromova Bay (Fig. 11) was about 1.5 m (information of resident C. Klochkov). (reference #10007)
The same maximum run-up height [1.6 m] was measured by resident V. Severyuhin in the south-eastern part of the bay near the local fire station. (reference #10007)
Maximum tsunami run-up near the recently built pier reached the pier level, i.e., 2.5 m above mean sea level or 2.4 m above the tide prediction (reference #10007)

The tsunami in Malokurilskaya Bay was observed as a sequence of sea level oscillations accompanied by strong currents and noise due to breakage of the floating ice. Eventually, some of the ice piled up on the coast and some was sucked back to the sea by the draw-down current. A Navy officer, Seminutin, reported about the tsunami behavior on 11 March in the northern part of the bay near its neck: ‘‘After tsunami alarm at 16:20 local time (06:20 UTC) we marked the initial water level position by an iron pole. The sea level rose about 0.3–0.5 m at 07:05–07:07 UTC. Minutes later the water level started to drop and the water flowed from the bay with the speed of 6–8 knots. Intensive current oscillations were continuing until the afternoon of March 12 for in and out flow directions. The peak run-up occurred at about 19:05–19:10 local time. It was measured later around 20:00 local time (10:00 UTC) as 1.6 m above mean sea level or 1.5 m over tide prediction’’ (reference #10007)

According to a report submitted by Inspector of the National Park ‘‘Kurilsky’’, Yu. Sinkevich, and residents Vasiliev, Tomason and Severyuhin, the tsunami oscillations in Otradnaya Bay were not significant. The tsunami broke thick ice in the bay only near the coast. Sea water deposited black sand over snow near the shoreline. Consequently, the inundation limit was clearly visible, and run-up heights were measured within a 0.5–2.0 m range. (reference #10007) Note: >180 m inundation listed but unclear if this was upriver and/or on land

The tsunami brought heavy ice into the lower part of the Krabozavodskoye settlement and deposited it in Torgovaya Street (Fig. 17). The bridge near Torgovaya Street (1.2 m above mean sea level) was covered by sea water. The tsunami height in this area was estimated as to be approximately 1.5 m. (reference #10007)

Volkov, a teacher in the middle school in the Krabozavodskoye settlement, provided a detailed description of the tsunami behavior with a number of photos made after 08:30 UTC. ‘‘At about 18:30 of local time (08:30 UTC) the sea water receded dramatically about 25 m seaward. Thereafter, the water started to rise and at 18:50 the usual sea level was exceeded by approximately 2 m. At 19:10 the water level was a little lower than the new pier in the port. At 19:30 local time, sea level dropped about 3 m and the sea floor under half of the old pier became dry. Later, sea level rose to the previous highest position. Next morning, March 12, from 09:20 to 09:40 local time (23:20 to 23:40 UTC, March 11) sea level rose 1.5 m above mean sea level. From 09:40 to 10:00 local time (23:40 to 24:00 UTC, March 11) sea level dropped to 1.5 m below mean sea level’’. Measurements made near the old pier gave 2.0 m for the maximum sea level drop relative to mean sea level.
The port area of Krabozavodsk covered by the sea water.
The tsunami caused damage in the Port of Krabozavodsk. A fuel pipe was cut by floating ice, and sea water coming into the ground floor of a dormitory deposited piles of sand and rubbish inside the building
(reference #10007)

However, fluctuations within 20cm can be typically caused by meteorological conditions, so tsunami information was not issued. (reference #13584)

properties.COMMENTS: The fifth, Saanich Peninsula Group , are the stations located around the Saanich Peninsula (Figure 13d). The specific properties of the respective records is that only the “direct” wave arrivals (indicated in Figure 19 by red arrows) is evident. The wave from the Pacific Ocean propagated through Juan de Fuca Strait, came into the southern Strait of Georgia, went through Haro Strait along the eastern coast of the Saanich Peninsula and at 17:44 UTC (i.e. 13 hrs and 29 min after the Tonga Hunga eruption and 26 min later than at Victoria) the tsunami wave was recorded at Saanichton. Then, 7 min later, it arrived at Sidney and 2 more min later into Tsehum Harbour. It is interesting that because of some topographic amplification, the maximum measured tsunami wave at Tsehum Harbour was even higher than at Saanichton: 22.9 and 20.6 cm, respectively (Table 7). The dominant period at all these three stations was very stable: 50 min. [...] Going around the northern end of the Saanich Peninsula, the tsunami wave, strongly attenuating, penetrated into Saanich Inlet and was recorded in Patricia Bay and at Bamberton; (reference #13594) Note: “Direct wave” as defined by reference #13594 as “oceanic waves radiating outward from the source at the longwave speed”

Reference #13607:

Part of a railroad embankment, for 275 ft (85 m), slumped into Patterson [sic] Lake south of Lacey (loc. 140) during or shortly after the 1949 earthquake. The slide is reported to have caused a wave surge that rose 10-12 in. (25-30 cm) over a nearby dock. Approximately 25,000 yds3 (19,000 m3) of material was required to repair the damage (U.S. Army Corps of Engineers, 1949). The failure involved artificial fill over Vashon glacial sediments.

“We really felt it bad on S.E. side of Lake Patterson [sic]. As I sat up after the shaking ground threw me, I saw the last cars of a freight train go over the trestle across the lake, then the land slid from under the tracks and at the same time the water rose over dock (10 or 12 inches) [25 or 30 cm] ”(Mrs. Harry A. Esborg, written commun., 1949).

Note: based on description it is likely the authors refer to Pattison Lake, not Patterson. Pattison Lake is just south of Lacey, WA, with a railroad track along side. While Patterson Lake, in north-central Washington, is ~250 km northwest of Lacey.

properties.COMMENTS: On the 19th of April, the Seismic Research Center of the University of West Indies (SRC/UWI), in charge of the volcano monitoring, reported that PDCs descended the western flank of the volcano and reached the Caribbean Sea. The Caribbean TSP, once informed by SRC/UWI, observed a 10-cm high tsunami on a tide gauge located to the south coast of St Vincent

A report in the November 19, 1929, issue of the New York Times states, “The Long Island shore was lashed by an extraordinarily high tide, however, which broke over sea walls and inundated the roads, marooning many automobiles hub-deep in water.”
It must be noted that at the time of the earthquake there was a strong nor’easter that affected the New England coast. Nor’easters are often accompanied by storm surges that can overtop sea walls and cause coastal flooding. Furthermore, the 1929 earthquake took place at a time when the ocean tidal fluctuations were larger than normal. Thus, for Boston and New York, it is not clear how much of the flooding was due to the tsunami and how much was due to these other influences.

Reference #13702:
Hokuriku Electric Power Company on Tuesday released the results of its analysis of data from the water-level gauge near the Shika plant's seawater intake as well as the wave gauge near its wharf.
The utility said a tsunami measuring about one-meter high reached areas near the intake and wharf at about 4:35 p.m., 25 minutes after the quake struck. It said a wave about 3-meters high were observed there at about 5:45 p.m.
Other tsunami waves are thought to have reached the site multiple times.
Hokuriku Electric said the waves did not cause safety problems at the plant, which is built 11 meters above sea level and has a 4-meter-tall seawall.
At the Shika plant, some of its systems that receive electricity from outside are not functioning after pipes of transformers sustained damage in the quake.
The operator said on Tuesday that it discovered damage to some elements of equipment in a substation and power transmission lines. But it said the damage has no impact on the plant's operations.

Reference #13703:
The analysis of the tsunami became available after Hokuriku Electric collected data from an offshore measuring device that had stopped transmitting its records after the quake.

Note: measuring device does not appear to be a coastal tide gauge, rather an offshore device. Listed as “Tide Gauge” in database as it is not in “deep ocean”. Unclear if 3 meter measurement is height or amplitude. Damage from earthquake.

Reference #13704 states that near the confluence of the Seki River and its tributary, the Hokura River, the tsunami that ran up the river overcame the levees, and by the 9th, 15 houses along the river were confirmed to have been inundated. A research group led by Tomoya Shibayama, a professor at Waseda University who specializes in coastal engineering, estimated from the video footage taken that the tsunami that moved up the Sekigawa River was approximately one meter high near the river mouth.

Reference #13704 states that on the 5th of this month, a field survey was conducted at Funami Park, located on the seafront about 600 meters west of the mouth of the Seki River, and tree branches and seaweed were found near the entrance to the building and at the fence separating the park from the beach, which are believed to have been washed ashore by the tsunami. Professor Shibayama analyzed that the maximum run-up height of the tsunami reached 6.58 meters above sea level in the vicinity of this park. Professor Shibayama will analyze in detail the reason why the tsunami was locally higher. He believes that the relatively shallow seafloor off the coast of Joetsu City may have concentrated the tsunami, and that the tsunami may have been reflected by the cape, causing it to rise higher.
