properties.LOCATION_NAME: RV SIKULIAQ AT RESURRECTION BAY, AK
properties.COMMENTS:
12 cm maximum wave height (peak to trough). Some of the mountainous debris fell into Resurrection Bay, where the R/V Sikuliaq was in port (~ 650 m away from the landslide), generating a small wave. The small wave generated by the Lowell Point landslide was detected by the R/V Sikuliaq [equipped with Precise Point Positioning (PPP) of Global Navigation Satellite System (GNSS) receiver]. (reference #13716)

The GNSS receiver aboard the R/V Sikuliaq recorded the waves generated by the landslide, with a maximum wave amplitude of 6 cm and wave periods between 40 and 50 s (reference #14029)

Note: this is not a tide gauge observation, rather a ship in port equipped with a Precise Point Positioning (PPP) of Global Navigation Satellite System (GNSS) receiver.
Reference #13722 lists on May 7 at Bequia, one of the Grenadines, in Barbados, where it arrived at 3 h. 10 [local time] (amplitude of 75 centimeters),

Reference #13722 states the sea penetrated inland up to about 50 meters and destroyed around twenty houses at Petite Anse; we saw furniture and mattresses transported by the wave to the foot of the cliff which rises behind the Great Anse. A boat located a few miles from Carbet, at the time of the arrival at sea of the fiery cloud in this town, did not feel any movement of the sea. In Fort-de-France, the effect produced was was identical to that of May 8; it was the same in Trinite

Reference #13722 states that at Carbet, the amplitude was a little less than on May 20; entered the village of Delle-Fontaine, where it demolished a house. It was reported as having risen about a hundred meters inside the village of Case-Pilote, and 30 meters in that of Schoelcher.
In Saint-Pierre, must have exceeded 3 meters in amplitude (reference #13722)
Reference #13722 states a movement of the sea with an amplitude of 0.6 was noted from 8h 30 to 8h 50 at Fort de-France

Reference #13737 states that the tsunami has hit the Sirius Patrol's station [on Ella Island], where some material has been washed into the water. However, the station was abandoned for the season. There were therefore no people present, and therefore no injuries. Personnel from the inspection ship Knud Rasmussen, together with the Sirius patrol, subsequently started a clean-up work, which has now been completed.

At the Nanok station and research base at Ella O, 72 km away out-fjord, the tsunami had a local runup height of 4 m, inundating up to 80 m inland, and destroying infrastructure valued at nearly 200,000 USD. Note: At Ella O, a detailed runup height was mapped on a 2.59 cm/pixel DEM and orthophoto produced from drone images recorded on 10 September 2022. Using this dataset and photos recorded the day after the tsunami by the Danish Army, a detailed runup height could be reconstructed here. (reference #13837)

properties.COMMENTS: The effects of the seiches were noticed in the rivers and bayous of the New Orleans area where considerable damage was done to many boats and barges, which slammed against piers or were torn from their moorings. Most accounts indicate that water oscillations had peak-to-peak amplitude of approximately 6 ft (1.8 m) with a period of oscillation on the order of 5 seconds [...] Water disturbances “were not particularly noticeable” along the Mississippi River (Baton Rouge Morning Advocate, Mar. 28, 1964). There were reports, however, of boats breaking from their moorings in Venice, Louisiana. (reference #13762)

The Amite River, east of Baton Rouge, had peak-to-peak oscillations on the order of 4 ft (1.2 m) for a duration of 20 minutes [...] In Baton Rouge, the water in swimming pools, including the pool on the fourth floor of the Capital House Hotel, was disturbed. (reference #13762)

Note: seiches

properties.COMMENTS: In Valletta, Malta, ships in the harbor were violently shaken while in Alexandria the earthquake set up waves in the harbor and in canals (Ambraseys et al., 1994). The account that in the harbor of Valletta ships were violently shaken indicates rather a seiche than tsunami wave. The estimation of tsunami intensity in the QLC concerns the tsunami-like waves observed in Alexandria. (reference #13474)

At the bay of Camara de Lobos, a fisherman lost two fishing crafts. Despite having climbed a ramp of 15 m height, the fisherman and his co-workers were still caught by the wave. The fisherman’s house, where several families lived, was flooded through the window even though it is located at 15 m above sea level. (reference #13778)

Reference #13786: “Sargodha.—Mr. J. Middleton, Assistant Engineer. One continuous shock at first rapid to and fro and gradually getting slower but larger oscillation. Three and a half minutes’ duration Direction W.—E. by punkah and by water in irrigation channels. It was distinctly felt. He went outside hastily. After the shock there was a tidal wave came down the canal N.—S. No sound.” (p. 218)

properties.COMMENTS: The tsunami appeared harmless in this area, as no significant damage was observed, as confirmed by our interviews with local eyewitnesses. At location 4, a wooden building restaurant, known as Takoya restaurant, was situated approximately 45 m from the sea on a low-lying, unprotected beach. Remarkably, it remained unharmed by the tsunami, confirming the relatively small impact of the tsunami in the Himi area. (reference #13789)
A minor damage to the stepped revetment was spotted at survey location number 5 (Kozakai Beach), prompting authorities to cordon off the area. (reference #13789)

In locations 21 (Nagashima Island) and 22 (Yanami fishing port), tsunami was minimal and only small debris were observed allowing a tsunami height measurement of approximately 1.0 for both locations (Fig. 13). Strong coastal defenses were in place at both locations comprising of concrete seawall, tetrapod armour and stepped concrete revetments (Fig. 13). (reference #13789)

In locations 21 (Nagashima Island) and 22 (Yanami fishing port), tsunami was minimal and only small debris were observed allowing a tsunami height measurement of approximately 1.0 for both locations (Fig. 13). Strong coastal defenses were in place at both locations comprising of concrete seawall, tetrapod armour and stepped concrete revetments (Fig. 13). (reference #13789)

In Ukagawa (location 17), a tsunami height of 2.0 m was measured where we were guided by clear tsunami debris at this location. This part of the Sea of Japan coast involved a coastal road protected by a concrete seawall. It was evident that the seawall was not overtopped by the tsunami because the area behind the wall was clear and tidy (reference #13789)

Unoura port (location 15) sustained damage from both the earthquake and tsunami, though distinguishing between the two causes proved challenging (Fig. 11). Several large cracks were observed on port structures which were likely generated by the earthquake shaking. (reference #13789)
Damage due to tsunami inundation currents and water pressure were spotted in locations 8 and 9. (reference #13789)
Damage due to tsunami inundation currents and water pressure were spotted in locations 8 and 9. (reference #13789)

We observed typical damage to buildings from tsunami current pressure and debris impacts at location 10, along with the accumulation of tsunami debris behind the seawall (Fig. 15). Such accumulation of debris behind the seawall can be attributed to tsunami backwash. Despite a tsunami height of 3.7–3.9 m in this area and overtopping of the seawall, it is important to note that the seawall itself sustained no damage, which can be attributed to the high-quality construction of the structure. (reference #13789)

Near the Misaki elementary school (location 14), tsunami debris was found on a bridge handrail, which also sustained damage from debris impacts, prompting us to measure a tsunami height of 3.7 m. (reference #13789)
Damage noted (reference #13789)
At location 12 (Jiketsu-1), coastal houses were damaged and tsunami watermarks were clear on the inside walls of the buildings (reference #13789)

Damage to metal fences, and glass doors of buildings were observed (reference #13789)

4.5 runup (reference #13791)
At location 13, tsunami debris such as large tree parts and household utensils were observed, facilitating a runup measurement of 5.0 m. Note: damage noted (reference #13789)

The concrete and rock units on the detached breakwater appeared intact and no apparent movement could be seen by our visual inspection from the shoreline. This may indicate that the tsunami was small and harmless with a height of probably less than 1 m at these three locations. (reference #13789)

The concrete and rock units on the detached breakwater appeared intact and no apparent movement could be seen by our visual inspection from the shoreline. This may indicate that the tsunami was small and harmless with a height of probably less than 1 m at these three locations. (reference #13789)

The concrete and rock units on the detached breakwater appeared intact and no apparent movement could be seen by our visual inspection from the shoreline. This may indicate that the tsunami was small and harmless with a height of probably less than 1 m at these three locations. (reference #13789)

In locations 6 and 7, no damage or clear tsunami watermark was observed (Fig. 11), making it impossible to determine the tsunami height (Table 2). The Enotomari fishing port (location 6), was operating normally at the day of the survey (25 days after the earthquake) confirming that the tsunami was negligible at this site. It is worth noting that a significant new landslide was observed in the mountains near the port, likely triggered by the January 2024 Noto Peninsula earthquake (Fig. 11). Note: it is anticipated that tsunami heights were less than 1 m [at this location] (reference #13789)
Note: it is anticipated that tsunami heights were less than 1 m [at this location] (reference #13789)

We were unable to find any tsunami-related damage in Maenami fishing port (location 16), although earthquake-related damage was evident here in the form of several large cracks on the concrete slabs of the port structures (Fig. 12). Since no tsunami watermark was visible, it was not possible to measure the tsunami height in location 16. properties.COMMENTS: The record in Gibraltar indicated a train of oscillations with maximum troug-to-crest height of about 3.5 cm beginning at about 07:00 UTC, December 27, i.e. about 30 hrs after the main Sumatra shock. However, the visible period of these oscillations (~1.5 hrs) is by my opinion too large for tsunami waves. (reference #13801)

properties.COMMENTS: In Le Havre (Manche, or British Channel), the waves (10 cm peak to trough) are observed a few hours after beginning of 28/12. This is consistent with a slow WE propagation in the Channel, a rather shallow area (hardly deeper than 50 to 100m). (reference #13802)

properties.COMMENTS: The waves have also been observed in Brest, La Rochelle, Cherbourg, but the highestare observed in Concarneau (reference #13802)

properties.COMMENTS: 16 Pillar Mandapam. At around 09:45 the sea begun to recede and there was no water between the jetty and Vivekanand Rock Memorial and the Thiruvalluar statue. A similar situation had never occurred in the past. Around 11:00 large sea waves started hitting the coastline and destroyed a number of ships and other structures. The waves continued to hit for about 20 to 25 minutes. The whole event lasted for about two and half hours. One boat at Kanniyakumari jetty was swept away and was found after two months at Earnakulam. (reference #4082)

properties.COMMENTS: The tsunami peak at Chala (0.20 m) occurred 15 min after the earthquake, and the following waves did not exceed this height. (reference #14018)

the response of the population to the tsunami alert was generally erratic and often disastrous. Most coastal residents sought to evacuate over excessive distances, in motor vehicles, and often along the main available road, i.e., in a direction parallel to the coastline, which is obviously inefficient in terms of evacuation. As a result, there was chaos in densely populated areas such as Toamasina, where the gendarmerie reported numerous traffic accidents, with six fatalities. (reference #4288)

The man who was in the skiff pulling in the sea line, was drove with it a considerable distance over the flat, and grounded upon a small eminence until the water subsided. There were three successive swells, as at Otter Creek, and the effects up the creek were the same, with this difference, the water only rose seven feet. In both cases, the lake, after the three swells had spent their force, gradually subsided, and in about twenty minutes was at its usual height and tranquillity. properties.COMMENTS: Staci Lehman, spokeswoman for the Washington state Department of Fish and Wildlife, said the wave hit strong enough to dislodge a dock at Sherman Creek Hatchery, which is north of the slide. The wave sent a dock and several fish pens full of triploid rainbow trout for a ride. Sherman Creek Hatchery is located on the west side of Lake Roosevelt, the same side as the slide. It’s also located up a creek from a bay, meaning that the wave had to have come inland some way before it caused the damage. “We are not positive when it happened,” Lehman said. “One of our employees went to check on the net pens on Sunday morning. According to interviews of people present at the Sazanami fishing port, some facilities, such as trucks and forklifts, were partially damaged by the tsunami.
Interviews with local residents revealed that the tsunami curiously reached the Sazanami area within a few minutes after the earthquake occurred, although this area is far from the landslide trace detected by the Japan Coast Guard survey. A resident living in front of the fishing port told us that he began preparing for evacuation in his car immediately after feeling the earthquake shaking and observed the fishing port’s boats sinking (not in water) as the water level receded due to the incoming tsunami waves. Typically, eyewitness accounts of tsunami arrival times are vague, and it is difficult to determine specific times. However, in this area, multiple residents remember the unusually early arrival time of the tsunami, which suggests unique circumstances.

properties.COMMENTS: A report from Cyprus, dated 4 April 1743 and reviewed by Ambraseys and Finkel (1995), says that “. . . I have been informed from Satalia (Antalya) that from the 8th to 20th of the month there were terrible earthquakes as a result of which the port dried up for some time, many houses collapsed as well as part of the walls at different places which fell on the consul’s house, destroying it. Many villages were lost in this earthquake and a mountain opposite that, which lies west of the islet of Rachat (Re at), sunk completely”. This report is rather convincing as for the strong destructive earthquakes that shook the area of Antalya to the east of Rhodes. However, the piece of information that “the port dried up for some time” does not imply beyond doubt that there was a tsunami. (reference #2840)

According to BRGM (2013) , who quotes a report of Philosophical Transaction of the Royal Society of London, an eye-witness report that on June 4th at Bonne "...half one hour before the sunset a sudden extraordinary current of the sea happened. In less than a minute the sea water retired and sunk ten feet and upwards. The sea shore become dry more than two hundred paces from its common mark, leaving the fish upon dry land, number of which were taken up; .....Three minutes after, the waters entered again with the same rapidity, with which they ran out; and I observed even till night, that those irregular motion of the sea diminished by degrees; and that, about every two minutes, the waters went in and out alternately, loosing their motion insensibly, like those undulations made by agitating a vessel of water." properties.COMMENTS: [...] tsunami signals occurred at Trincomalee tide gauge at 14:35 UTC, so the tsunami wave travel time was ~ 10hrs and 20 min.). The pressure fluctuations travelled for ~ 09 hours and 40 min over 11,500 km from Tonga to Sri Lanka (strait distance) with a speed of 320 ms-1. However, it takes approximately 17 hours for long free waves to travel from Tonga to Sri Lanka (~13,000km) with a wave speed (C=√(gh) of 210 ms-1 (h=average water depth of 4500m between Sri Lanka and Tonga). Therefore, the observed sea-level fluctuations can be considered as meteotsunamis forced by the pressure perturbation rather than formed at the erupted region and propagated as free wave. (reference #13887)

properties.COMMENTS:
Reference #13893:
After 3 October 1883 (south-west Malekula). Following an earthquake, three tidal waves swept the southwestern coast of Malekula from the west. The amplitude of the tsunami was about 2m (14 feet from trough to crest; Wawn, 1893, in Louat and Baldassari, 1989). The eyewitness, William T. Wawn, who was on board a ship anchored in the channel between Ura Islet and the south-western coast of Malekula, described the scene reported below,
"At either side, on the shallow reefs, and high over the low bushes and smaller trees that lined the shore, a huge wave was breaking, sweeping steadily along the coast from westward, until it disappeared beyond a long, low point of land. It was the swell of this wave, unbroken in the deeper water, which had caught the ship aft, and had slewed her round to her anchor. On the islet we could hear the yells and cries of the natives, as they fled from an adjacent village, making for higher ground. On the main island, cloud of dust could be seen for miles away, showing where landslips has occurred on the side of the steep hills and mountains. For miles the whole surface of the earth had subsided, sinking eight feet or so, which had caused the great wave to rush into the deepened channel. Then, slowly and gradually, came an upheaval. The water poured out from the flooded forest, bearing with them portions of the huts of the savages, canoes, trees and branches, and even two or three squeaking pigs, cascading over the face of the flat shore reefs. These now rose as high above their normal position as they had before sunk below it, forming flat terraces along the coasts, which were elevated to six feet above the surface of the sea. Masses of “Live” coral showed along the face of the raised shore-reefs, displaying brilliant hues, blue, green, yellow, purple, and red, all shining and glistening in the sun. This was the first act. A pause of a minute followed. Then, gradually and majestically, the upraised coral sank again, and the bright colour disappeared. Then came another subsidence, and a second vast billow rolled in from westward, making our chain rip and tear at the bows as if it meant to pull the windlass out of the ship. Breaking into clouds of foam, the wave ran roaring along the shores, while every here and there some huge tree came toppling over, with torn root or broken trunk. The second upheaval was not equal to the first; the reefs did not rise more than about three feet above the water. Though a third wave rolled in, it was only a “piccaninny” (small) when compared with those that had preceded it. When the earthquake was over, I could perceive no difference in the height of the shore, from the level of the sea. The only effect remaining visible were the branches and broken trees floating about, or lying strewn along the beaches, with here and there, a bare yellow brown patch on the side of the hill."

"...About half-past three o'clock on the Monday morning we had another shock of earthquake, much heavier, though greatly shorter, than the first, and which brought down the stone chimney in our cook-house, and which, I presume, was the shock that damaged the stone church at Anelgauhat. About five o'clock, a little before daylight, there was a third, not so heavy as either the other two; and about eight o'clock there was a fourth, which some thought to be heavier than any of the former three; but as all the damage had be done by the second that could be done, without a considerable additional force, this fourth shock left no special traces of its presence. from that time for more than three weeks there was not a day in which there was not one or more shocks. During the first ten days they amounted to upwards of a hundred; a good many of them were rather sharp shocks, but none of them doing any damage. So far as my experience and information go, the law of earthquakes seems to be this: - All the damage is done by the first shock or shocks; these again, are succeeded by a number of lighter shocks, which inflict no serious injury. After the severe earthquake in Wellington in 1848, while we were living there, there was not a day for three months without one or more shocks, but they did no damage; and we then learned that some old whalers had had a similar experience at Dusky Bay many years before [...] I should have mentioned that on the Monday morning the natives found a considerable number of fish of various kinds left high and dry by the receding wave; also one large turtle and several young ones not half grown: these latter are very rarely seen or caught together.” from Inglis, Rev. J., 1887. In the New Hebrides. Reminiscences of missionary life and work. T. Nelson and Sons, London. (reference #13894)

I reached our house and had just got the key, when I heard a great angry roar. On opening the door of the room, to my horror I saw a prodigious wall of sea, stretching right across the bay, and which appeared about forty feet high, come rolling in. That instant I heard Watata calling : " Misi, the sea, the sea is coming! Never mind the boat. Escape with your wife and child for your lives ! " I sprang into the bedroom, caught up the child and wrapped her in a blanket, and, with Mrs. Robertson, rushed out at the backdoor. The native girls were standing terror-stricken just outside, and I told them to follow us. I called to Watata to chain the boat to a tree. Fortunately he heard me and did so, and then, with the Erromangans, made for the high ground at the back of our cow-shed. On his way he called to an old woman named Lalim — the mother of Navusia, Yomot's wife, who was living near us — to run for her life. But she refused to leave her charms and sacred stones ; and climbing on a pile of stones near her house she held on like grim death to them and to her heathen baubles. She escaped, but only by about five feet. We ran straight to the hill at the back of our house. As we began the ascent, it seemed, from its dreadful roar, as if the sea was right upon us. It had then reached the stone fence in front of our house. We bounded from rock to rock and rushed through the reeds and scrub, till Mrs. Robertson, getting entangled in them, fell. I called back to her to run. [Note: damage descriptions included in reference]

At Hiratsuka, large villages have been deployed on the sand bar that extends in the Sagamigawa River mouth area since the ancient times. In some views, no tsunami was caused there by the Great Kanto Earthquake, but actually the above-mentioned Oiso suffered tsunami damage and a tsunami as high as 3 m or so struck Fujisawa, too. It is unnatural to claim that only Hiratsuka remained unaffected. Historical Material A attempted to omit the description of the tsunami at Hiratsuka without listing it as an item by combining it with Oiso. Probably no information about the tsunami at Hiratsuka was available by that time. On the other hand, since tsunami has a nature of going up a river to expand its flood area, it highly likely went up the Sagamigawa River at Hiratsuka, too. The recently found oral handing-down had it that “the tsunami wave went up to Yonno-Miya.” The Yonno-Miya District is situated 4 km upstream from the current river mouth and is measured around 9 m above the sea level. Therefore, we can reconstruct that the tsunami at Hiratsuka was as high as 3 m or so the same as in the neighboring towns and that it reached the location 9 m above the sea level. (reference #13917)

Reference #13956:
NOA’s tide gauge in Kasos, which supports the operations of the Hellenic National Tsunami Warning Center (HL-NTWC, one of the three Tsunami Service Providers operating in the Eastern Mediterranean), picked up what appears to be a very small tsunami. No other tide gauge in the region showed any sea level excitation after the earthquake. Given the noise-level wave amplitudes of the Kasos tide gauge record, tsunami-ongoing messages were not issued by the Tsunami Service Providers, and the authors are not aware of sightings of tsunami waves or currents being reported.

Whilst the ratio values are evenly distributed across the frequency range of the plot, which is further evidence that if any tsunami signal exists it is close to background level, the peaks at 6.6 and 9.8 min period stand out in that the rise in energy is not narrow-peaked.\

From the analysis of the Kasos tide gauge record, it cannot be concluded with certainty whether a (small) tsunami was recorded or not since the signal after the earthquake remains close to the background noise level. The oscillation energy marginally increased after the earthquake, but this alone does not prove the presence of tsunami waves, since storm waves could also have contributed. If tsunami waves were indeed recorded, the sign of first-wave arrival is the generation of spectral energy in the 6–10 min period range starting at ∼ 18 min after the earthquake, and peaking at the arrival of the first distinguishable drawdown of the water level at∼39 min after the earthquake. The wavelet and periodogram analyses thus suggest that any tsunami spectral energy from the source would lie primarily in the 6–10 min period range.

Legend has it that Jamesto,vn, Nevis' original capital, sank beneath the sea in a great earthquake on April 30, 1680. What is more likely, however, is that the 1690 earthquake was the culprit. No evidence has been found of any such occurrence in 1680, and the name of Jamestown appears in public records and on maps for up to a century after the supposed disappearance took place. What is more likely is that Jamestown was heavily damaged in 1690, and the population gradually moved to other parts of the island. It has been said that ruins have been seen under the sea in that area from time to time when the sands shift, and that at night under the full moon a church bell can sometimes be heard tolling beneath the waters.

According to local legend and lore, Jamestown vanished in 1690, destroyed by a tsunami.
Tessa Machling, historian with the Nevis Heritage Project, has assembled documents from the National Archives in London that suggest that Jamestown’s rise and fall was tied more to the fortunes of sugar than the terror of wind and wave.
The place name ‘Morton’s Bay’ then disappeared, supplanted by ‘Jamestown’, probably to honor the future English king James II (1685–8).

However, for 1690 the picture is less certain: an earthquake did occur in April of this year (Robson 1964). An eyewitness account of the event (Anonymous 1690) describes the sea retreating from the land before returning again with great force. It also mentions that many houses in Charlestown were destroyed. However, the account makes no mention of Jamestown or its destruction. It also does not mention the destruction of any fort. In fact Charles Fort is described as having 'escap'd' damage. In fact, none of the other low-lying forts on Pinney's Beach report any destruction. In a further account by Governor Christopher Codrington, although much of the island's stonework is described as damaged (Christopher Codrington, PRO CO152/37:4/6/1690), no record is made of a lost town or fort.
Had the town and fort been lost it would surely have merited some comment, particularly in the dangerous years of the late seventeenth century when the easiest landing place on Nevis (John McArthur, PRO CSP 1702, No.132) would have been left undefended. Indeed, following later disasters, such as the French attack of 1706, numerous petitions, accounts of damages, etc. were sent to England. In Jamaica, where an earthquake in 1692 caused the destruction of the town of Port Royal, many accounts of the disaster survive (Pawson and Buisseret 1975). No such documents could be located for the 1690 Nevis event.
In addition to the overwhelming documentary evidence, recent geological work carried out in the area, although preliminary, has not been able to locate any tsunami related deposits (Andrews 2001: 68).
The origins of the earthquake story appear to be found in a history of Nevis made by a Nevisian planter, John Alexander Burke Isles. Burke Isles was a Justice of the Peace and had been Colonial Secretary in the 1870s. In 1871, he wrote his 'An Account Descriptive of the Island of Nevis, West Indies' (Burke Isles 1871). Typically Victorian, the account makes mention of great disasters, heathen savages and great wars, all written in a flamboyant and extravagant prose.

Mr. Fotis Fragias, born in 1940 and a native of Asprogerakas village, east Cephalonia (Figure 7), was an eyewitness to the earthquake and the associated tsunami that happened in the early morning of 12 August 1953. On 15 February 2014, the son of Mr. Fotis Fragias uploaded his father’s narration, which reads as follows: “At that morning, along with my brother we were prepared to go fishing. Being onboard we had raised anchor in the small and shallow harbor of Poros, exactly at the place the earthquake started. We saw the sea water withdraw from the harbor like a river. We were scared that a hole opened in the sea floor sucking the water. We immediately dropped the anchor back so that we would not be towed away by the stream. The waters continued to leave until all the ships sat on the sand, and the harbor was empty of water. It was the tsunami beginning but at that time we had ignorance of the phenomenon. After a few minutes, keeping the impression that some hole sucked up the water, we feared the dust in the mountains caused by the earthquake; then we saw the sea moving again filling the harbor and washing everything. Some of our colleagues began running in panic and climbing to higher points, believing that the island could be sinking!!! Then the water receded once more, and came back again with greater intensity, until at some point it stopped. It again receded for a little, the water level remaining at least 40 cm lower since then and remains so until today”. The previous account implies not only the generation of a strong tsunami in Poros Bay but also the permanent co-seismic uplift of the coast. An eyewitness, Mr. Theologos Vavlas, a school student at the time, on 14 May 2014 narrated the inundation of the tsunami observed after the earthquake: “In 1968, in the Pasalimani site [eastern Kos], where “Tarzan” beach is situated today, the tavern “Paraskevas” was there. There suddenly the sea swelled and rose up, the wave was as high as about 1.00–1.20 m, and because of this our houses flooded. We were forced to go up to the roofs because we were afraid of. The incident happened in the morning around 8 or 9, if I remember correctly [earthquake local time 9:52 a.m.]. In the port boats broke, others were found on the streets while my neighborhood was flooded. The water was stagnant for 4–5 h and wouldn’t go away, only after days it receded. It was not bad weather, and the phenomenon appeared suddenly. I recall it was a calm day and we woke up in the morning and saw the water in our houses, with the people being upset. In the port, the old houses and shacks of the port were damaged. My mother was worried and wanted to take us up to the mountains. Where the carnage used to be, the wave swept ships and boats up to the arch [Phoinikon Avenue Bridge]. In the harbor there are still 2–3 boats that sank since then"
It is of interest that the eyewitness did not mention earth-shaking at all, which is reasonable since the tsunami observation point lies at an epicentral distance of ~45 km. Since the earthquake was not of very large magnitude, combined with the fact that the wave was observed only in one coastal spot, we may suggest that the tsunami likely was generated by a submarine landslide caused by the earth-shaking close to the Kos port.
[During a field survey in 2017] we observed one small fishing boat lying exactly at the spot of the arch in Phoinikon Avenue Bridge. Initially we considered that it was removed there by the 20 July 2017 tsunami. However, after talking with local people, we verified that this boat was abandoned there for many years. This is consistent with the fact that the boat was in a situation of significant deterioration. Very likely, it was one of the boats that, according to the narration by the eyewitness of the 5 December 1968 tsunami, was removed ashore. [...] It is of interest that the eyewitness did not mention earth-shaking at all, which is reasonable since the tsunami observation point lies at an epicentral distance of ~45 km.

Reference #14020 (unofficial translation):
The first historical record was written by Alvar Nunez Cabeza de Vaca (1555). A group of Spaniards leaving Buenos Aires and heading for Asunción in 1542, on what would be the current coast of Colonia, in Uruguay, in the ravines near the mouth of the San Juan River (today's Estancia Presidencial Anchorena), experienced an earthquake and probably a seiche that caused the death of at least fourteen people.
After a failed attempt to refound Buenos Aires, following the evacuation of the city of Buenos Aires in 1541 (Schávelzon, 2006), Gonzalo de Mendoza made a second attempt in 1542 to refound the city. But the harsh winter made it difficult, so they decided to return to Asunción. On the way, they anchored off the coast of Uruguay, at the mouth of the San Juan River, Colonia, with its coastal ravines.
On Saturday 31 October 1542, the eve of All Saints' Day, something disastrous happened to Captain Gonçalo de Mendoça. He lost a ship loaded with goods and provisions and many people died. He writes that something strange happened while they were sailing. That day before, his ships were anchored on the river bank. Among them was a galley tied to a tree. He says that the earth shook, and the earth itself came down like a blow from the sea into the ravine. The trees fell into the river, and the ravine struck the brigantines, and the tree where the galley was tied gave such a blow to the galley that it pushed the ship upside down. And so it was dragged more than half a league (approximately two kilometres), with the mast underneath and the keel on top. In this event, fourteen people, including men and women, drowned in the galley and in the other boats.
It is difficult to estimate the magnitude of the earthquake from this information, but it is certainly the strongest earthquake ever recorded in the region.
And if it happened once, it is possible that one of similar magnitude could happen again. The fact that at least fourteen people died, in an open field, at a time when the region was virtually unpopulated, speaks to the significance of this event.

Reference #14019 (unofficial translation):
On the eve of All Saints' Day, when the ships were lying on the banks of the river near some high ravines, and the galley that Goncalo de Mendoca, the earth trembled and the earth itself came rolling down as if it were a sea blow to the ravine and the trees fell into the river and the ravine hit the gullies and the tree where the galley was moored gave such a great blow to the galley that it knocked it upside down. And so it carried her more than half a league, filling the mast below and the quinilla above, and this storm drowned in the galley and other vessels fourteen persons, men and women. And according to what those who were present said, it was the most fearful thing that ever happened. And with this labour they arrived at the city of the Ascension, where they were well provided for and supplied with all that was necessary. And the governor and all the people gave thanks to God for having brought them to safety and escaped from so many dangers as they had passed along that river.

Reference #3460:
At 1600 hours on 15 August, the presence of the anomalous swell that had been predicted by this Directorate in Special Notice 37 dated 12 August can be clearly observed. The first wave of the tsunami arrived 54 minutes after the earthquake (19:34 hours), reaching a height with respect to mean sea level of 1.04 m, which if we reduce the effect of the anomalous swell, decreases to 0.74 m. However, the highest waves (1.08 m), arrived at 21:47 and 00:10 hours, originated by the combined effect of the increase in the intensity of the swell, the final oscillations of the Tsunami and the resonance of the bay itself. [note: translation from original Spanish supported by AI tools]

Reference #3460:
In this port, no flooded areas were detected, nor material damage or loss of life due to the tsunami, however, the tide gauge station located at the pier of the San Juan Naval Base, allowed us to observe the pattern shown in the tide gauge record [...] At 1500 hours on 15 August, we can clearly observe the presence of the anomalous swell that had been predicted by this Directorate in Special Notice 37 dated 12 August. The first wave of the Tsunami arrived 31 minutes after the earthquake (19:34 hours)[note: this arrival time is a typographical error and should be 19:11, as can be noted by marigram image on pg. 14], reaching a height with respect to the mean sea level of 0.77 m, which if we reduce the effect of the anomalous swell, reached 0.67 m. Finally, from the analysis of the whole time series of the mentioned tide gauge record, it was obtained that the average speed at which the Tsunami wave moved was 320 km/h, a period of 10 to 15 minutes and a wave length of 80 km. [note: translation from original Spanish supported by AI tools]

Another recorder on the ocean coast was in Dimitrov Bay on Shikotan Island (distance from Hanasaki station is about 115 km). Here the nature of the wave process was somewhat different, more typical of bays with a system of stable resonant oscillations, when instead of a powerful single wave a wave train with a maximum amplitude in the center of the group was observed. The maximum (96.5 cm) was noted at 04:05, and the minimum (–91.5 cm), at 04:15. Thus, the wave height from crest to trough was 188 cm. This was the strongest manifestation of meteotsunami on the coast of the Kuril Ridge and even in the entire Russian Far East. It corresponds to the parameters of a moderate intensity tsunami (which includes tsunamis with a wave height smaller than 2 m). Such a wave can pose a real danger to ships and coastal infrastructure facilities located near the shore. However, it was observed on the Pacific coast of the island, where there is currently no permanent population. (reference #14028)

Note: bottom hydrostatic pressure recorder; location approximate

[...] significant oscillations here began with a negative phase (−51.2 cm at 03:38, a few minutes earlier than in the neighboring basin), and the maximum of 34.6 cm was observed at 03:51, the wave height from the trough to the crest was 85.8 cm. This wave began a group of seven oscillations, among which the third was the smallest (50 cm), and the sixth, the largest (the maximum was 41.4 cm at 5:16, the minimum was −61.2 cm at 5:26, the wave height was 102.6 cm). Four more groups of waves were associated with the meteotsunami, the amplitudes of which gradually decreased. The last group was observed from 18:30 to 22:20 UTC, the maximum height in it was 34 cm, which is also not a small value. The main energy of the oscillations is concentrated in a narrow frequency band from 0.05 to 0.07 cpm, and only at the very beginning of the first wave packet the low-frequency boundary of significant spectral amplitudes reached 0.04 cpm. (reference #14028)
Note: bottom hydrostatic pressure recorder; location approximate

On Kunashir Island, after relatively weak fluctuations, a pronounced positive maximum of 51 cm was noted at 04:26, which occurred almost half an hour later than in Otradnaya Bay. The reason for such a time shift for closely located stations is unclear. The minimum was recorded at 04:44 and amounted to 16 cm. Slowly decaying fluctuations were observed in these bays for about 11 h. (reference #14028)

The strongest difference in the wave process in the first of them was that it began with a pronounced negative phase (the minimum was –34 cm at 03:43), and was followed by a powerful positive maximum of 57 cm at 03:58 (slightly earlier than in Dimitrov Bay). (reference #14028)

It is quite difficult to determine the moment of the meteotsunami arrival. Most likely, it can be attributed to 00:41 UTC, when the nature of the oscillations changed, the intensity of high-frequency components decreased and variations with a period of about 30 min began to dominate in the records. The maximum wave (+53 cm relative to the zero average level) was recorded much later, at 01:27, the subsequent minimum (−17 cm) at 01:44. Thus, the wave height from crest to trough was 70 cm. Reference #14100 [unofficial translation]:
It was the Benedictine monk Friar Gaspar da Madre de Deus who first reported that several buildings in Vila de Sao Vicente didn't last long because the sea took everything away (Madre de Deus, 2010). Much later, the historian Mario Neme (1954), when discussing the controversy over the location of the old Porto das Naus, near the town of Sao Vicente, suggested that the disaster could have been caused by a tsunami or a strong surge/agitation/swell [term used in the publication is “ressaca”]. [...] More recently, Eduardo Bueno (1999) relived the episode, saying that a tsunami submerged a large part of the village, when witnesses saw the arrival of waves eight meters high that advanced inland for around 150 meters, destroying houses and other buildings. He reproduced the map of the flooded area drawn up by Mario Neme, but didn't say how he estimated the height of the waves and their advance on the mainland. However, Friar Gaspar's writings reinforce the idea that the waters arrived suddenly, with no time to remove anything: “[...] 50 reis were spent to remove the bells from the sea and the pillory from the beach; 20 reis to transport them to the new town and 250 reis to rebuild the pillory with stone, clay and water”.

Reference #14100 [unofficial translation]:
Residents of the ancient city of Bahia, now Salvador, experienced an unusual event: “the sea rose three times in three alternating days, with such a profusion of water that it ran over the limits that nature had set for it, expanding the waves far beyond the beaches, and leaving them covered with countless small fish, which the residents of the city and the suburbs harvested” (Pitta, 1950). The historian adds that the inhabitants were more concerned with looking after their appetites than imagining how the sea had “voluntarily and lavishly brought them such a copious tribute” [...] The special thing about this account is the triple repetition of the phenomenon on alternate days.

Reference #14100 [unofficial translation]:
On the evening of May 9, 1789, “without a breath of wind, the small and peaceful sea that surrounds Cananeia became rough, and its waves crashed furiously against the beaches” (Santos, 1922) [...] The historian noted strong waves and their impact on the terrain: “the waves crashed furiously against the beaches” around Cananeia. This may mean that the sea advanced over a significant stretch of beach, beyond its normal limit, with ebb and flow movements, similar to a small tsunami. Cananeia has a peculiar geographical position, as it is located at the head of a narrow, relatively shallow inlet, far from the coast. There, the waters are likely to be calmer than those of the coastline. In the event of a nearby earthquake, its effects would be much more pronounced in the calm waters around the city than in other locations on the open coast. Apparently, that ancient marine disturbance was produced by a localized tsunami, and the tremor that caused it possibly occurred in the sea, not far from the city.

Reference #14104 [unofficial translation]:
The sea also showed signs of the impact, because at that moment, without any wind, the little and peaceful sea that surrounded the village, produced waves that were impressive for being able to crash at the shores despite the calm atmosphere. The fish also demonstrated how weird this “impulse” was, because they were observed to be agitated, jumping outside of the water.
